subjects.title: Academic & Professional English
subjects.subtitle: Reading, writing and speaking with precision
subjects.summary: The craft of reading, writing and speaking in an academic register: paragraph logic, claims that match their evidence, honest citation and clear presentation. It decides whether sound engineering is understood and trusted.
subjects.text: The craft of reading, writing and speaking in an academic register: paragraph logic, claims that match their evidence, honest citation and clear presentation. It decides whether sound engineering is understood and trusted. What makes English academic Academic English is a register built for one job: to make a claim another person could check. It prefers evidence to assertion, precise nouns to vague ones, and a calm tone that persuades by reasoning rather than volume. Three habits carry most of the work: - Define a term before using it. - Keep one main idea to a paragraph. - Signal how each sentence follows from the last. Verbs do more than adjectives — establish, indicate and contradict tell the reader what you are doing, while very and really add heat without information. Paragraphs have a job A paragraph is an argument in miniature. It opens with a topic sentence stating the claim, supplies evidence, analyses what that evidence shows, and links forward. The analysis proves you can interpret rather than merely report, so it should never be left implicit. A useful test: read only the first and last sentence. If they already state and conclude the idea, the middle is evidence. The commonest student fault is the evidence dump — three examples and no explanation of what they jointly prove. Comparison without confusion When a task asks you to compare, choose the criteria first, then apply them in the same order to both cases. Otherwise the reader must hold two mental lists and rebuild the comparison themselves. Keep the axis explicit: not "the two policies differ", but "both reduce emissions, though one changes the fuel and the other the route". Parallel grammar helps — if one half of a sentence starts with a verb, the other should too. The table is a quick reference for the connectors that do the heaviest work. Relationship Useful connectors Watch out for Hedging: the strength of a claim Academic writing separates the certain from the probable from the merely possible. Hedging is the wording that keeps a claim proportionate to its evidence, and it is precision rather than weakness. Compare "The results prove the policy failed" with "The results suggest the policy did not meet its target". The second is still clear, but its strength matches what two cases can support. Strong verbs need strong evidence; measured verbs suit interpretation. Ask what evidence would justify the stronger version. If it is absent, step down the ladder. Claim strength ladder demonstrates indicates suggests may reflect Paraphrasing and citation Paraphrasing restates an idea in your own sentence structure, not by swapping synonyms inside the original order. If a reader could rebuild the source sentence from yours, it is still copying. Read the passage, close it, write the idea from memory in one sentence, then compare and cite. Even with every word new, the idea needs a citation, because ideas have owners too. Author–date referencing is standard in engineering reports: name and year in the sentence, full details in the list. Four checks for a paraphrase meaning kept + structure new + wording your own + source cited Speaking and signposting A presentation is a guided tour of your own argument. Give the route at the start, mark each turning point, and summarise at the end. Phrases such as first, this leads to and to conclude are road signs that let a listener hold the structure in working memory. Speak to the back of the room, slow down on numbers, and let silence do the punctuation. One clean visual per idea beats a dense slide, and in group talks the handovers need rehearsing — a clumsy transition is more noticeable than a small stumble. subjects.title: Innovation & Entrepreneurship
subjects.subtitle: Turning an engineering idea into something people use
subjects.summary: How a technical idea becomes something people actually use: finding a real problem, testing it cheaply, shaping a value proposition and a business model. It is the commercial grammar behind engineering projects.
subjects.text: How a technical idea becomes something people actually use: finding a real problem, testing it cheaply, shaping a value proposition and a business model. It is the commercial grammar behind engineering projects. Innovation is not invention An invention is a new idea; innovation is that idea made useful, adopted and repeated. A patent that never leaves the laboratory is an invention. A cheap sensor network a site team uses every day is an innovation. - Most innovation is incremental: a better joint, a faster inspection, a leaner mix. - Disruptive innovation changes the cost or access of a whole market, not just the performance of a product. - Incremental ideas need testing and feedback; disruptive ones need protection and patience. Start from a problem Engineering projects often begin with a technique looking for a use; entrepreneurial ones begin with a person and a difficulty. The useful question is not "what can we build?" but "whose work is harder than it needs to be, and why?" Observation beats assumption. Watch how people do the task, note the workarounds they have invented, and ask what they lose when it goes wrong — time, money, safety or reputation. A pain point that recurs weekly beats a feature that sounds clever. The empathy map organises the first round of interviews. Empathy map Says · Thinks · Does · Feels Design thinking as a cycle Design thinking reduces the risk of building the wrong thing. It moves through empathising with users, defining the problem, generating alternatives, building a rough prototype and testing it with real people. The cycle repeats; it is not a single pass. The define step is where most projects fail. "Site supervisors cannot see which deliveries are late until the crew is already idle" is testable. "Improve construction efficiency" is not. Cheap prototypes early are worth more than polished plans late. Design thinking cycle Empathise → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test → repeat Value proposition and business model A value proposition states who the customer is, what job they need done, and why your offer does better than the alternatives. The pains you relieve and the gains you create should each be tied to a specific user. A business model answers the harder questions: who pays, for what unit, how often, and what it costs to deliver. Engineering firms sell expertise and assurance rather than an object, so the model is often fee-based and reputation-driven. Question Value proposition Business model Smart city technology in construction The technology layer is where civil engineering meets data. Cheap IoT sensors report temperature, vibration, dust, water level or equipment hours, giving earlier warning of a failing pump, curing concrete or a worker in a restricted zone. Artificial intelligence adds pattern-finding: predictive maintenance, flagged unsafe sequences, and schedules adjusted for weather and deliveries. Blockchain concerns records more than site work — an auditable chain of custody for materials and certificates. Adoption is the hard part. A sensor without backup power fails in a fire, and an alarm that cries wolf gets switched off. Technology earns trust only when it is reliable, maintained and tied to a decision someone owns. From idea to venture A minimum viable product is the smallest version that can generate real feedback: a landing page, a paper prototype, a single pilot site. It is built to learn, not to impress. Funding follows evidence. Many ventures start with founders' savings and early customer payments, then move to grants, competitions or angel investment as traction appears. Each source buys time at a price: equity, reporting duties or restrictions. Teams also need a legal structure, accounting, insurance and a view of regulation. Most first ventures fail on weak demand or running out of cash, which is why fast, honest feedback beats a perfect plan. subjects.title: Leadership & Teamwork
subjects.subtitle: Working with people when the stakes are real
subjects.summary: How people actually work together: communication loops, empathy and I-statements, the stages every team passes through, and the feedback that keeps conflict useful. Engineering projects are delivered by teams, not by calculations.
subjects.text: How people actually work together: communication loops, empathy and I-statements, the stages every team passes through, and the feedback that keeps conflict useful. Engineering projects are delivered by teams, not by calculations. Communication is the work On a project, most failures are not calculations. They are information failures: a drawing revision nobody opened, a risk raised in a meeting but never recorded, a worker who misunderstood the sequence. Communication is a technical skill, not a personality trait. A sender encodes a message, chooses a channel, a receiver decodes it, and feedback closes the loop. Noise — jargon, a noisy site, a rushed message — enters at every stage. A one-way broadcast with no feedback is not communication; it is an announcement. Communication loop Sender → Message → Channel → Receiver → Feedback Empathy and I-statements Empathy is the attempt to understand another person's position before responding to it. It is usually split into: - affective empathy (feeling a response to emotion) - cognitive empathy (working out what someone is thinking) - compassionate empathy (being moved to help) In engineering teams the cognitive kind does most of the work: it predicts where misunderstanding occurs. When something goes wrong the temptation is a you-statement such as "you keep sending late drawings". It assigns blame and invites defence. An I-statement describes the behaviour, the feeling and the concrete impact, and leaves the other person room to act. I-statement When [behaviour], I feel [feeling] because [impact]. Teams pass through stages Teams rarely become effective by announcement. They pass through recognisable stages, and the leader's job changes with each one. At first people are polite. Disagreement follows, and that is normal: roles, standards and authority have to be negotiated. Only then can shared habits settle. The practical lesson is to expect the dip. A team that argues in week three is often healthier than one that stays agreeable and never tests an idea. Stage What it looks like Leadership focus Roles and social loafing A group is not automatically a team. Teams work when each person has a clear, distinct contribution and everyone can see who is doing what. When responsibilities blur, social loafing appears: individuals reduce effort because the link between their work and the outcome is invisible. - Give every task one named owner and a visible status. - Make contributions reviewable. - Rotate the role of challenger so that disagreement becomes a duty rather than a risk. None of this survives without psychological safety — the shared belief that raising a problem will not be punished. Conflict and feedback Conflict about the work is often productive; conflict about people is corrosive. The aim is not to remove disagreement but to keep it on evidence and consequences. Constructive feedback describes what happened, what effect it had and what to do differently, without labels. The SBI pattern keeps it observable: situation, behaviour, impact. "In yesterday's briefing the pile locations were not mentioned, so the crew arrived at the wrong area" is something a person can change. "You are careless" is not. Timing matters as much as wording: feedback given close to the event, in private, is heard; feedback saved for an annual review is a verdict. SBI feedback Situation + Behaviour + Impact + next step Leadership without a title Situational leadership matches the amount of direction and support to the person and the task: a new task needs clear instruction, a familiar task needs delegation. Transformational leadership works through purpose and example; transactional leadership works through clear exchange. Most leaders mix both. Engineers often lead without authority — coordinating a consultant, chasing a subcontractor, persuading a client. subjects.title: Structural Mechanics
subjects.subtitle: How structures carry load, and how they deform
subjects.summary: The grammar of structures: how loads travel through members, how stress and strain relate, and how beams, shafts and columns fail. It underpins every later design subject.
subjects.text: The grammar of structures: how loads travel through members, how stress and strain relate, and how beams, shafts and columns fail. It underpins every later design subject. Start with a free body diagram Every structural question begins the same way: isolate the part you care about, draw every force acting on it, and apply equilibrium. A free body diagram is not decoration — if a reaction or a member force is missing, the numbers that follow are meaningless. For a planar structure there are three independent equilibrium equations: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0 and ΣM = 0. Use them to find reactions first, then cut the structure at the section you need. The internal forces at a cut are always drawn in their positive sense: axial force N, shear force V and bending moment M. A structure is statically determinate when the reactions can be found from equilibrium alone. Extra supports make it indeterminate, and the solution then needs compatibility — the requirement that deformations fit together. Planar equilibrium ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣM = 0 Stress, strain and the elastic modulus Stress converts a force into an intensity: normal stress σ = F/A acts perpendicular to the section, while shear stress τ acts along it. Strain is the corresponding deformation per unit length, ε = ΔL/L. For a linear elastic material, stress and strain are proportional up to the yield point. The constant is Young's modulus E = σ/ε, a measure of stiffness rather than strength. A material can be stiff but weak, or flexible but strong — steel is both stiff and strong; rubber is neither stiff nor strong, but it is very extensible. When a bar is pulled, it also gets thinner. Poisson's ratio ν = −εlateral/εaxial captures that effect, and it links the elastic constants: G = E / [2(1 + ν)]. The value of ν for steel is about 0.30 and for concrete about 0.15–0.20. Normal stress σ = F / A Young's modulus E = σ / ε Shear modulus G = E / [2(1 + ν)] Axial deformation and compatibility A prismatic bar of length L, area A and modulus E carrying axial force P changes length by ΔL = P L / (A E). This is the workhorse of indeterminate problems: write the elongation of each member in terms of the unknown force, then impose the geometric condition that the members still meet at the same joint. Temperature change adds a free expansion ΔL = α L ΔT. If that expansion is restrained, the member develops a thermal stress σ = −E α ΔT. A steel rail fixed at both ends on a hot day is in compression even though nothing touched it — the movement was prevented, not the temperature. Axial deformation ΔL = P L / (A E) Thermal stress, fully restrained σ = −E α ΔT Bending: the flexure formula Bending moment produces a stress gradient across a section. The neutral axis passes through the centroid; fibres on one side are in compression and on the other in tension. The flexure formula is σ = M y / I, where y is the distance from the neutral axis and I is the second moment of area about that axis. The maximum stress occurs at the extreme fibre, so a section is often described by its elastic section modulus Z = I / ymax, giving σmax = M / Z. Doubling the depth of a rectangular beam increases I eightfold, because I = b h³ / 12 — depth is far more efficient than width. Shear force does not disappear. In a beam it produces a parabolic shear stress distribution, zero at the extreme fibres and maximum at the neutral axis, with τmax = 3V/(2A) for a rectangle. Flexure formula σ = M y / I Elastic section modulus Z = I / ymax Second moment of area, rectangle I = b h³ / 12 Deflection and the stiffness check Bending also changes shape. The curvature is related to the moment by EI v'' = M, where EI is the flexural rigidity and v is the transverse displacement. Integrating twice gives slope and deflection; the constants come from the supports. For common cases the results are worth remembering: - Simply supported beam with central point load P: δ = PL³/(48EI) at midspan. - Simply supported beam with uniformly distributed load

subjects.title: AI & Data Analysis
subjects.subtitle: Finding patterns in data and reading them honestly
subjects.summary: Data is only as good as the questions asked of it. This page covers describing a dataset, fitting and judging a regression line, and spotting the quality problems that make a confident answer wrong.
subjects.text: Data is only as good as the questions asked of it. This page covers describing a dataset, fitting and judging a regression line, and spotting the quality problems that make a confident answer wrong. Data before models Analysis begins with what was recorded, not what software can do. Each variable is a measured property — compressive strength, chloride content, delay in minutes — and its type sets the legal arithmetic: - nominal labels can only be counted - ordinal ranks ordered - interval values subtracted - only ratio scales have a true zero Most engineering data are a sample from a larger population, so every summary is an estimate. Ask how rows were selected; a convenient sample measures the sampling method as much as the subject. Summarising a dataset The first pass is descriptive and cheap: centre, spread and shape. The mean is the balance point, the median the middle value, and the mode the most frequent category. Spread is reported as the standard deviation, which shares the data's units, or the coefficient of variation, which is dimensionless and comparable across variables. Skew drags the mean towards the long tail while the median barely moves, which is why repair costs and rainfall are quoted as medians; keep the sample size beside any summary. Sample mean x̄ = (Σ xᵢ) / n Sample standard deviation s = √[ Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² / (n − 1) ] Coefficient of variation CV = s / x̄ Statistic What it summarises Where it misleads Correlation is neither a slope nor a cause Plot first. Two variables can follow a clear curve and still return a correlation near zero, because the Pearson coefficient r measures only linear association. It is unit-free, runs from −1 to +1, and is not a slope: r = 0.9 does not tell you how much y changes per unit of x. Correlation is not causation either. A third factor can drive both variables, the causal arrow may run backwards, or the sample may be selected on the outcome. Randomisation, a control group or a natural experiment licenses a causal sentence. Pearson correlation coefficient r = Σ(xᵢ−x̄)(yᵢ−ȳ) / √[ Σ(xᵢ−x̄)² · Σ(yᵢ−ȳ)² ] Fitting a line by least squares A simple linear regression fits ŷ = a + b x by choosing the line that minimises the sum of squared vertical gaps between each observation and the line. Squaring treats positive and negative misses alike and punishes large misses hardest, so one outlier can tilt the fit. The slope b is the predicted change in y per one-unit increase in x. The intercept a is the prediction at x = 0, which is often outside the measured range and physically meaningless. Quote both with units, and never present an extrapolated prediction as if it had been measured. Least squares slope b = Σ(xᵢ−x̄)(yᵢ−ȳ) / Σ(xᵢ−x̄)² Intercept a = ȳ − b x̄ Judging the fit The coefficient of determination R² is the share of the variation in y that the model accounts for: 1 means every point lies on the line, 0 means the model is no better than predicting the mean. It says nothing about whether the form of the model is right — a curve fitted over a narrow range can still score well. Residual plots are the honest test. A pattern means the model is misspecified, a funnel means the variance changes with x, and a handful of very large residuals flags influential points. Report typical error, not just R². Coefficient of determination R² = 1 − SSres / SStot Testing a model honestly A model is useful only if it performs on data it has not seen. Split off a test set before tuning, or cross-validate when the sample is small; otherwise the model can memorise the training rows and appear excellent. For a numeric prediction, report the mean absolute error or the root mean square error, both in the units of y; the root mean square penalises large misses more heavily. A low error on a well-chosen test set is evidence; a low error on the training set is arithmetic. Root mean square error RMSE = √[ (1/n) Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)² ] Data-quality pitfalls Most modelling failures are data failures. Missing values may be mi

subjects.title: Air & Noise Pollution
subjects.subtitle: Measuring, modelling and managing what we breathe and hear
subjects.summary: What we breathe and what we hear are both energy problems, measured in concentrations and decibels and controlled by understanding how a pollutant travels from source to receptor. This page covers air-quality units and dispersion, then environmental noise.
subjects.text: What we breathe and what we hear are both energy problems, measured in concentrations and decibels and controlled by understanding how a pollutant travels from source to receptor. This page covers air-quality units and dispersion, then environmental noise. Source, pathway, receptor Air and noise problems share one structure: something emits, the emission travels and changes, and a receptor is exposed. Control can act at any stage: - Source: cleaner fuel, process changes - Pathway: taller stack, barrier - Receptor: insulation, land-use separation The earliest option is usually the cheapest. A tall stack is not a treatment device: it lowers ground-level concentration by spreading the same mass through a larger volume — the pollutant is diluted, not destroyed. Measuring what is in the air Concentrations are reported as mass per volume (μg/m³) or volume fraction (ppm or ppb), linked through the gas's molar mass using a molar volume of 24.45 L at 25 °C and 1 atm. The instrument matters as much as the number: - Gravimetric samplers: weigh filtered particulate matter; reference method - Real-time monitors: reading every few seconds; need calibration - Passive diffusion tubes: cheap; integrate over weeks Averaging time is part of the result: a one-hour peak and an annual mean describe different effects. Volume fraction to mass concentration C (μg/m³) = C (ppm) × M × 1000 / 24.45 Dispersion: the Gaussian plume Once released, a plume spreads by turbulence. The standard screening model treats concentration as Gaussian across the wind and vertically, with spread parameters σy and σz that grow with distance and depend on atmospheric stability. Stability is graded from class A (very unstable, strong convection) to class F (very stable, clear and calm). Unstable air mixes strongly and lowers ground-level peaks; a stable night traps the plume near the ground. The effective stack height H adds plume rise from buoyancy and momentum to the physical stack, and it dominates because concentration falls roughly exponentially with H. Gaussian plume, ground-level centreline C = Q / (π u σy σz) · exp[ −H² / (2 σz²) ] What the plume model assumes The Gaussian model is a screening tool. It assumes steady wind, flat terrain, no building downwash, no chemical reaction and a single source, so it is best used for comparing options rather than for proving compliance. Where those assumptions fail the error is large: valleys and street canyons trap pollutants, an inversion caps the mixing depth, and reactions form secondary pollutants such as ozone well downwind. A real assessment adds terrain correction, a measured background and monitoring. Controlling air pollution Control options fall into prevention, collection and dilution: - Prevention: cleaner fuel, low-NOx burners, process changes, energy efficiency - Collection: cyclones for coarse dust; electrostatic precipitators and fabric filters for fine particles; wet scrubbers for soluble gases; catalytic converters on vehicles - Dilution: tall stack — last resort, turns a local problem into a regional one Siting decisions and buffer zones are planning controls, and often the most effective. Air quality management and the health account Measurement exists to be compared with an objective. Air quality management sets objectives for each pollutant — annual and short-term limits for particulates, nitrogen dioxide, ozone and sulphur dioxide — and reports the comparison publicly through an index that translates measured concentrations into simple bands and health advice. The health account explains why the objectives matter: fine particles penetrate to the deep lung, ozone irritates the airways, and the burden falls most on children, the elderly and those who already have heart or lung disease. Management therefore acts on exposure as well as emissions: an emission inventory identifies the sources, dispersion modelling maps who is exposed, and the control plan reduces the highest-exposure source first. subjects.subtitle: The industry, the project team and the work itself
subjects.summary: Construction turns drawings into a built asset through a temporary organisation of clients, designers, contractors and suppliers. This page follows a project from procurement through site work, safety, programme and cost control to handover.
subjects.text: Construction turns drawings into a built asset through a temporary organisation of clients, designers, contractors and suppliers. This page follows a project from procurement through site work, safety, programme and cost control to handover. Projects, not products Construction is organised project by project. Each site assembles a one-off product in the open air, using labour and plant that move on when the job ends. The industry is fragmented: a few large contractors sit above many small specialist subcontractors and suppliers, and much of the work is done by small firms. That structure explains the familiar risks: - Design and construction are separated - Decisions pass through many hands - Weather and ground conditions interrupt the programme - Margins are thin - Much of the knowledge sits with people rather than with the product The project team Every project has a client who pays and defines the need, a design team that turns the need into documents, and a contractor who builds. On the design side: - The architect arranges the spaces - The civil and structural engineers make the ground and frame work - Services engineers size the systems - The quantity surveyor measures and prices the work On site: - The contractor's project manager runs the programme - The commercial manager watches cost - The site agent runs the day-to-day work - A clerk of works or inspector checks that what is built matches the approved design - The regulator grants consents to build and occupy Procurement: how the work is bought Procurement decides who designs, who builds and who carries which risk. - Traditional (design–bid–build): the client's consultants finish the design and contractors tender on it; the design is settled before prices are committed, but change is slow and the relationship can turn adversarial. - Design–build: one contract for design and construction, shortening the programme and placing design risk with the builder, at the cost of less client control. - Construction management: brings a contractor in early to manage packages, which suits complex or fast projects but leaves the client carrying more cost risk. Underneath all three sit the payment terms — lump sum, remeasurement or cost plus — each shifting risk. Route Who designs Cost certainty Strong when Temporary works Temporary works are the structures that make the permanent work possible: formwork and falsework to shape and support wet concrete, scaffolding for access, shoring and props for excavations, crane bases, piling mats and edge protection. They carry real loads and fail like real structures. The discipline is procedural as well as structural. A temporary works coordinator keeps a register, each scheme is designed and checked in proportion to its risk, and striking — removing the support — waits until the concrete has gained enough strength, judged from test results rather than the calendar. Load paths must run continuously from the new work down to the ground. Concrete practice: mix, place, cure Concrete arrives ready-mixed or is batched on site, and a mix is defined by its proportions rather than its brand. The key ratio is the water–cement ratio: the mass of free water divided by the mass of cement. Strength falls as the ratio rises, because the surplus water leaves capillary voids behind; a workable mix and a strong mix pull in opposite directions, and admixtures exist largely to reconcile them. Consistency is checked with a slump test, the classic site quality control. Placing follows with compaction to expel trapped air, and curing — keeping the surface moist and shaded for days — lets hydration continue. A member stripped early and left to dry never reaches the strength its cubes suggest. subjects.subtitle: How flight works and how airports are engineered
subjects.summary: How aircraft fly and how the ground system that supports them is engineered: the four forces, lift and stall, runway and terminal constraints, air traffic separation, and the industry's environmental account.
subjects.text: How aircraft fly and how the ground system that supports them is engineered: the four forces, lift and stall, runway and terminal constraints, air traffic separation, and the industry's environmental account. Four forces, one balance Flight is a balance of four forces: lift upward, weight downward, thrust along the flight path and drag against it. In steady level cruise lift equals weight and thrust equals drag; any imbalance changes speed, altitude or both. - Lift grows with air density, airspeed squared and wing area. - Density falls with altitude and rises in cold air. - Runway performance therefore depends on the day's temperature and pressure, not just the aircraft. Lift L = ½ ρ V² S CL Steady level flight L = W, T = D Drag D = ½ ρ V² S CD Angle of attack and the stall The angle of attack is the angle between the wing chord and the oncoming air. Lift rises with it until the airflow can no longer follow the upper surface; beyond the critical angle the wing stalls and lift drops sharply. A stall is about angle, not speed. - Flaps and slats raise low-speed lift at the cost of extra drag, so they are retracted for cruise. - Induced drag falls as speed rises, because less angle of attack is needed for the same lift. - Total drag therefore has a minimum at one speed, where the lift-to-drag ratio is highest and range is longest. Lift-to-drag ratio L/D = CL / CD Navigation aids and the instrument approach Aircraft navigate by a chain of aids: - VOR radiates bearings so a receiver can hold a radial. - DME adds distance. - Satellite navigation fixes position anywhere with no ground station. - The instrument landing system guides the final approach with localiser and glide slope beams followed to the runway threshold. An instrument approach is a choreographed sequence: the arrival route feeds a published approach procedure, the aircraft intercepts the localiser and glide slope, and stabilisation gates check speed and configuration at fixed heights. If the runway is not in sight at the decision height, the approach is abandoned and a designed missed approach procedure flown. Instrument approach sequence arrival → approach procedure → localiser intercept → glide slope → decision height Aid What it provides Limitation The flight deck and its instruments Six basic instruments tell the pilot the aircraft's state, arranged in the classic T-pattern: airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and vertical speed indicator across the top, with heading and turn coordination below. Modern glass cockpits merge them onto screens, but the underlying quantities are unchanged: speed, attitude, altitude, rate, heading and turn. The instruments work on different physics — pitot pressure for speed, static pressure for altitude, gyros for attitude and heading — and that independence matters. When one disagrees with the others, the pilot cross-checks rather than trusting the odd one out; scan, interpret, verify is the discipline of the whole panel. The six-pack T-pattern airspeed · attitude · altitude · vertical speed · heading · turn Airports are engineered systems An airport separates two flows: aircraft on the airside — runway, taxiways and apron — and people and goods on the landside, meaning the terminal, road access and baggage system. Security and border control sit on the boundary. - Runway orientation follows the prevailing wind, since aircraft take off and land into wind. - Runway length is set by the most demanding aircraft and the worst conditions: high altitude, high temperature, a wet surface and an approach obstacle all lengthen it. - Capacity is rarely one number: runway movements, stands, check-in desks and baggage belts each impose a limit, and the airport's capacity is the tightest. subjects.subtitle: Bending, shear centres, torsion and buckling
subjects.summary: Load paths in members that are neither symmetrical nor circular: principal axes, shear centres, warping torsion and the stability of real columns. It explains why a channel twists and why a slender strut fails below its yield load.
subjects.text: Load paths in members that are neither symmetrical nor circular: principal axes, shear centres, warping torsion and the stability of real columns. It explains why a channel twists and why a slender strut fails below its yield load. Symmetry is the exception Textbook sections are usually symmetric, so the load plane and the neutral axis stay perpendicular and the two bending directions can be treated separately. Real members are less obliging: unequal angles, channels loaded off-centre, Z-purlins and crane rails all bend in a direction that matches neither centroidal axis. The coupling comes from the product of inertia Ixy = ∫xy dA, which measures how the area is spread through the four quadrants. When it is zero, bending about one axis produces no stress at points defined by the other coordinate and the simple flexure formula applies. When it is not, the neutral axis tilts. Product of inertia Ixy = ∫ x y dA Product of inertia and the principal axes For a section built from rectangles, Ixy sums each part as Ai x̄i ȳi, because a rectangle contributes nothing about its own centroidal axes. Doubly symmetric sections have Ixy = 0; a section with one axis of symmetry also has it zero about that pair of axes. The principal axes are the centroidal axes for which Ixy vanishes. Finding them is the same algebra as principal stresses: the angle obeys tan 2θp = 2Ixy/(Iy − Ix), and the principal second moments sit between the two extremes. Substitute the angle back to check which axis carries which value. Principal angle tan 2θp = 2 Ixy / (Iy − Ix) Principal second moments Iu,v = (Ix + Iy)/2 ± √[((Ix − Iy)/2)² + Ixy²] Stress in unsymmetrical bending With centroidal axes x and y, the normal stress at a point is given by the formula below, with both moments taken positive when they cause tension in the positive quadrant. The denominator is never negative, because Ix Iy ≥ Ixy². Setting σ = 0 gives the neutral axis: it passes through the centroid, but its slope is unrelated to either axis. The extreme stress is not automatically at the corner furthest in x or y, so check every corner. About principal axes the coupling vanishes and the familiar form returns, with σ = Mv u/Iv + Mu v/Iu. Unsymmetrical bending stress σ = [(My Ix − Mx Ixy) x + (Mx Iy − My Ixy) y] / (Ix Iy − Ixy²) Shear flow and the shear centre Transverse shear is not uniform. In a thin-walled section, cut the wall somewhere and balance the longitudinal force on the area beyond the cut: the shear flow is q = VQ/I, where Q is the first moment of that area about the bending axis, and the wall stress is q divided by the thickness. For a channel, the flange and web flows combine into one vertical force whose line of action is not the centroid. The point through which a transverse load produces no twist is the shear centre, a purely geometric property. For a channel it lies outside the web, away from the flanges, at e = 3b²/(h + 6b) from the web centre-line, with b the flange width and h the depth between flange centre-lines. An equal angle has its shear centre near the heel. Shear flow q = V Q / I Shear centre of a channel e = 3b² / (h + 6b) Section Product of inertia Shear centre Torsion beyond the circular shaft A circular shaft twists without warping, so τ = Tr/J and θ = TL/GJ are exact. Any other section warps: plane sections do not stay plane, and the simple torsion formula fails. A solid non-circular bar reaches its maximum shear stress on the boundary nearest the centroid, with the value taken from a coefficient table. A closed thin-walled tube carries torsion by circulating shear flow, so τ = T/(2Am t) and J = 4Am²/∮(ds/t), with Am the area enclosed by the wall mid-line. An open section has no closed path for the flow and is far weaker, J ≈ Σ(1/3)bt³. That is why a box resists torsion far better than an open channel of the same mass. Bredt shear stress τ = T / (2 Am t) Closed-tube constant J = 4 Am² / ∮(ds/t) Open-section constant J ≈ Σ (1/3) b t³ Struts and effective length A p

subjects.subtitle: Thinking in code: logic, data and functions
subjects.summary: A first course in thinking like a program: storing values, steering decisions, repeating work, packaging logic into functions, and moving data through files. These habits carry into every later computing subject.
subjects.text: A first course in thinking like a program: storing values, steering decisions, repeating work, packaging logic into functions, and moving data through files. These habits carry into every later computing subject. Values, names and types A variable is a name bound to an object, not a labelled box of fixed size. Python decides the type at run time: int for whole numbers, float for decimals, str for text and bool for True or False. Use type(x) when unsure, and convert deliberately with int(), float() and str(). The operator you choose changes the result. / always produces a float, // floors to an integer and % gives the remainder, which is the basis of many digit and parity tricks. Floating-point values are binary approximations, so test 0.1 + 0.2 and you will not get exactly 0.3; compare with a tolerance instead of equality. Quotient and remainder q, r = divmod(n, 10) Input, output and formatting input() always hands back a string, even when the user types digits. Convert before doing arithmetic, otherwise "7" + 1 raises a TypeError rather than giving 8. Formatting is part of the answer. Prompts and outputs often have to match exactly, so build them with f-strings: f"{day:02d}" zero-pads a day, and f"{total:.4f}" keeps four decimal places. A tidy program separates the prompt, the calculation and the display; mixing them makes debugging and marking harder. Reading a number n = int(input("Please enter a number: ")) Decisions with if, elif and else Conditionals choose a path, and every condition is just an expression that evaluates to true or false. Order the branches from most specific to most general, and add a final else only when every remaining case belongs there. Watch the classic mistakes: - = assigns while == compares - and binds more tightly than or - a test such as if name: is true for any non-empty string, which is often more than you intended Write the intended cases as comments first, then code them — that small habit removes most logic errors before they appear. Loops and the accumulator pattern A for loop walks over a sequence; a while loop repeats until a condition fails. Choose for when the number of items is known and while when it is not, and make sure the while condition can actually become false — a loop variable that never changes gives an infinite loop. The most reusable pattern in early programming is the accumulator: start a total at zero, add each item inside the loop, report after the loop. The same shape counts, sums, filters and searches. Keep the update line explicit so a reader can see exactly what changes and when. Accumulating a running total total = total + x Functions and recursion A function gives a name to a piece of logic, takes parameters and returns a value. Prefer returning a result over printing inside the function: returned values can be tested, reused and composed. Keep each function to one job and name it for what it does. Recursion solves a problem by calling a smaller version of itself. Every recursive function needs a base case that returns without recursing, plus a recursive step that moves towards it. A Fibonacci function is the standard demonstration, but recursion also suits nested structures where a loop would need its own stack. Recursive Fibonacci fib(n) = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) Lists, tuples and dictionaries A list is an ordered, mutable sequence indexed from zero, so a[0] is the first item and a[-1] the last. Slicing copies a section, while append, sort and remove edit the list in place. Because a list is shared by reference, b = a does not copy it; b = a[:] does. A tuple is an immutable sequence, useful for fixed groups such as coordinates. A dictionary maps keys to values and is the natural structure for counting, because it can create a key lazily instead of demanding a pre-check. Nested lists represent matrices: loop over rows first, then over columns. Counting with a dictionary counts[ch] = counts.get(ch, 0) + 1 Container Ordered Mutable Typical use Strings are sequence

subjects.subtitle: Concrete and steel, from composition to testing
subjects.summary: Concrete and steel as engineering materials: how cement hydrates, how mixes are proportioned and tested, and how steel behaves in tension. It links laboratory measurements to the durability decisions made on site.
subjects.text: Concrete and steel as engineering materials: how cement hydrates, how mixes are proportioned and tested, and how steel behaves in tension. It links laboratory measurements to the durability decisions made on site. Cement is a chemical system Portland cement is made by burning limestone and clay to a clinker, then grinding it with a little gypsum. The clinker contains four main phases: - Alite gives most of the early strength. - Belite contributes slowly over months. - Aluminate sets fastest and releases the most heat. - Ferrite adds little. Gypsum is the set regulator, keeping the aluminate from stiffening the paste within minutes. When water is added, the silicates hydrate into calcium silicate hydrate (the gel that glues everything together) plus calcium hydroxide. Strength is not a property of the powder; it is the product of a reaction that needs water, time and a controlled temperature. Water, setting and w/c ratio The water/cement ratio is the mass of water divided by the mass of cement, and it controls almost everything: workability, strength, permeability and shrinkage. Only about 0.23 times the cement mass is chemically bound at full hydration, but extra water is needed for workability, so practical mixes sit near 0.40–0.55. More water means more capillary space, and strength falls as w/c rises. Setting and hardening are different: setting is the loss of plasticity, hardening is the gain of strength. The Vicat apparatus finds the water content for standard consistency, then the initial and final setting times. Accelerators shorten setting, retarders lengthen it, and calcium chloride accelerates but risks reinforcement corrosion. Water/cement ratio w/c = mass of water / mass of cement Aggregates and mix proportioning Aggregate fills roughly 60–75% of the volume and provides the skeleton of concrete. Grading matters: a continuous range of sizes fills voids, reduces the paste needed and improves workability, while single-sized aggregate needs much more paste. Angular, rough particles interlock but demand more water; weak or absorptive particles limit strength and durability. Mix design works backwards from a target: - Choose a target mean strength above the specified characteristic value to allow for site variability. - Pick the w/c ratio that delivers it. - Fix the water content for the required slump. - Proportion cement and aggregates. Fly ash and slag replace part of the cement, lowering hydration heat and improving long-term performance. Target mean strength fm = fck + 1.64 s Workability, compaction and curing Workability describes how easily a mix can be placed and compacted without segregation. The slump test is the field check: a cone is filled in three layers, lifted, and the drop of the concrete is measured. A true slump is acceptable; a shear or collapse means the mix is unsuitable and must be repeated. Slump describes consistency, not strength. Compaction removes entrapped air — typically 2–5% of the volume if neglected, costing a similar share of strength. Curing keeps water available so hydration continues: about seven days of moist curing is normal, longer for hot, marine or low-w/c work. Poor curing leaves a weak, permeable surface layer, which is where durability problems begin. Steel: composition and tensile behaviour Structural steel is an iron–carbon alloy. Carbon raises strength and hardness but reduces ductility and weldability, so structural grades keep it low and rely on manganese and small alloy additions. Hot-rolled sections, plates, cold-formed sheet, reinforcement and fasteners are all steel products with different forming histories and properties. The tensile test defines the material: a linear region gives E ≈ 200 GPa, then a yield point, a plateau, strain hardening up to the ultimate strength, necking and fracture. Yield strength is the design property, the ultimate strength an upper bound, and the elongation at fracture describes ductility. Hardness tests give a quick correlation with tens

subjects.title: Engineering Geology
subjects.subtitle: Reading the ground before you build on it
subjects.summary: How rocks, structures and weathering shape the ground a project sits on, and how site investigation turns observations into a design model. It is the link between a geological map and a safe excavation.
subjects.text: How rocks, structures and weathering shape the ground a project sits on, and how site investigation turns observations into a design model. It is the link between a geological map and a safe excavation. The ground records its history A site is the end product of deposition, burial, deformation and weathering over geological time. Two boreholes a few metres apart can meet completely different conditions, because a fault, a buried channel or a weathering front can pass between them. The task in engineering geology is to build a ground model — a three-dimensional interpretation of what is there — and then to state how confident that model is. That model decides foundation type, excavation method, slope angle, dewatering and the risk allowance in the price. Most surprises on site are geological, and most of them were predictable from a map, a core log or a photograph. Vertical and effective stress σv = γ z , σ′ = σv − u Minerals: the working vocabulary A mineral is a naturally occurring inorganic solid with a defined composition and an ordered atomic structure. Rock-forming minerals are mostly silicates — quartz, feldspars, micas, amphiboles and pyroxenes — with calcite, dolomite, halite and clay minerals making up most of the rest. Identification uses hardness on the Mohs scale, cleavage, lustre, colour and streak, but for engineering the useful properties are hardness, solubility and the tendency of clays to swell. Quartz is hard and inert; calcite is soft and dissolves in acidic water; mica splits into flakes and weakens a rock along one plane. Mohs hardness scale 1 talc → 10 diamond Igneous rocks Igneous rocks crystallise from magma or lava. Slow cooling at depth produces coarse, interlocking grains — granite, diorite, gabbro — while rapid cooling at the surface produces fine-grained basalt or rhyolite, and explosive eruptions produce tuff and volcanic breccia. Intact igneous rock is usually strong and abrasive, which makes it good foundation material and hard excavation. Its weakness is the discontinuity pattern: cooling joints, flow contacts and later faults divide the mass into blocks. In humid climates granite weathers along joints into grus and then saprolite, so strong rock can sit above a soil-like profile only a few metres down. Sedimentary rocks Sedimentary rocks form from deposited material: clastic types such as sandstone, siltstone and mudstone, chemical and biological types such as limestone and chalk, and evaporites such as gypsum and halite. Their defining feature is bedding, and bedding planes are the surfaces along which the rock most readily separates, slides and leaks. Sandstone behaviour depends on its cement: silica-cemented sandstone is strong, clay-cemented sandstone is not. Mudstone is weak, slakes on exposure and loses strength when wetted. Limestone is strong but soluble, so acidic water opens joints into conduits and cavities, producing karst, sinkholes and very localised permeability. Metamorphic rocks Heat and pressure alter existing rocks without melting them. Limestone becomes marble, sandstone becomes quartzite, shale becomes slate, and deeper metamorphism produces schist and gneiss. New minerals grow in preferred orientations, producing foliation — the layered fabric that gives slate its cleavage and schist its sheen. Foliation makes the rock anisotropic: it is weaker and more deformable across the fabric than along it, and it controls how a tunnel or a slope fails. Marble is strong but dissolves like limestone, and some schists contain low-friction or swelling minerals that turn a stable excavation into a problem. True thickness from an outcrop t = w · sin θ Folds, faults and joints The attitude of a plane is described by its strike (the compass direction of the horizontal line on it) and its dip (the angle it makes with the horizontal, measured perpendicular to strike). subjects.title: BIM Management
subjects.subtitle: Digital models, information and the project lifecycle
subjects.summary: Buildings described as structured information rather than drawings: one coordinated model, defined requirements and a controlled way of exchanging data through every stage. BIM management is the discipline of making that information trustworthy.
subjects.text: Buildings described as structured information rather than drawings: one coordinated model, defined requirements and a controlled way of exchanging data through every stage. BIM management is the discipline of making that information trustworthy. The model is only half the subject Building Information Modelling describes a building through structured digital information, not a single clever file. Each discipline produces its own information container — a model, a schedule, a report — and those containers are brought together into a federated model that stays coordinated without merging ownership. A 3D picture is the visible part, but the value sits in the data attached to it: what an element is, where it belongs, what it costs, when it is installed and who is responsible. A model without defined uses and requirements is an expensive drawing. Dimensions: 3D to 7D The dimensions describe what is layered onto the geometry. - 3D is the coordinated spatial model. - 4D adds time by linking elements to construction activities. - 5D adds cost through quantities and rates. - 6D adds energy and sustainability analysis. - 7D covers operation and maintenance information. The names are shorthand for uses, not a maturity ladder: a project can use 4D without a 5D cost model. Adding a dimension means adding discipline: the schedule must be maintained, the cost data priced, the asset data structured. That is why BIM uses are agreed and scoped rather than assumed. Dimension stack 3D geometry → + 4D time → + 5D cost → + 6D energy → + 7D operation ISO 19650 and the requirements chain Modern BIM management rests on a chain of information requirements. Organisational requirements (OIR) set the strategy and cascade into asset information requirements (AIR) and project information requirements (PIR); together these become exchange information requirements (EIR) for each appointment. The appointing party asks; the delivery team answers with a BIM execution plan (BEP) describing how it will meet them. The same chain runs through the information model: the project information model is created during delivery, while the asset information model supports operation after handover. The discipline is delivering the right information, to the right people, in the right form, at the right time. Requirements chain OIR → AIR / PIR → EIR → BEP → TIDP + MIDP → information containers EIR and BEP: the contract for information The EIR defines what information is exchanged, when, by whom, to what level of detail and in what format. It must be precise enough to price and check; vague requirements produce models that nobody can use. Level of information need clarifies how much geometry, data and documentation is actually required at each stage. The delivery team answers twice. The pre-appointment BEP shows approach, capability and capacity; the post-appointment BEP sets out methods, standards, the CDE and the delivery plans. Task teams write TIDPs for their own deliverables; the lead consultant combines them into the MIDP. Level of information need Level of information need replaces vague detail labels: for each element and stage, state how much geometry, alphanumeric information and documentation each purpose requires. A door may need full 3D geometry at construction but only its fire rating, hardware set and maintenance interval at handover — more detail everywhere is a cost, not a virtue. Setting the level per purpose stops both under-modelling (a drawing pretending to be a model) and over-modelling (geometry nobody will ever read). In practice a team writes it into the EIR and BEP as a table of model elements against stages, so every author knows exactly when detail is due and can be checked against it. Level of information need need = geometry + alphanumeric information + documentation The common data environment A CDE is one source of truth for project information, with controlled workflows rather than a shared folder. subjects.title: 專業中文傳意
subjects.subtitle: 工程專業寫作、公函與匯報
subjects.summary: 為專業中文讀者而寫、而講：選對語域，讓讀者跟得上結構，並清楚交代對方要做甚麼。內容以繁體中文書面語書寫，輔以工程個案與練習。
subjects.text: 為專業中文讀者而寫、而講：選對語域，讓讀者跟得上結構，並清楚交代對方要做甚麼。內容以繁體中文書面語書寫，輔以工程個案與練習。 先決定語域 下筆之前，先判斷場合有多正式。語域是讀者期望的語言層次：公開通告、客戶公函與團隊即時訊息，各有不同的正式程度。 - 正式書面語多用書面詞彙；把日常廣東話口語搬進計劃書，讀者會覺得不合場合。 - 正式程度藏在細節裡：稱謂與結語、中性語氣、完整句子、不用俚語。 - 全篇保持同一層次；一份正式報告中突然出現一句聊天式句子，會顯得粗疏。 讓人願意回覆的電郵結構 專業電郵要快速回答四個問題：誰在寫、為何而寫、需要甚麼、何時需要。 - 第一句寫目的，第二段補背景，然後提出一個清楚的要求與期限。 - 主旨應寫明項目與行動，不要只寫「報告」兩個字。 - 稱謂要配合關係，段落要短，結尾有敬語與聯絡方法。 - 回覆時留在同一郵件串，副本名單要有意義，附件名稱要清楚。 - 若對方需要行動，要明說——委婉暗示很容易被忽略。 訊息五點檢查 目的 + 對象 + 行動 + 期限 + 語氣 報告與計劃書：先講結論 計劃書由決策者閱讀，所以先寫決定。可靠的結構依次是背景、目的、對象、程序、人手、預算與應變。 - 標題編號，一段一個重點，數字盡量用表格。 - 摘要不是可選項：它要在幾行內交代要求、成本與效益，細節放在附錄。 - 讀者三十秒內找不到「要求甚麼」，就可能不會批。 計劃書骨架 背景 → 目的 → 程序 → 預算 → 應變 精簡才顯得可信 長句有時只是掩蓋了空白。 - 能用動詞就不要用沉重的名詞片語；刪去「有關方面」之類的虛詞；刪掉之後意思不變的句子，一律刪。 - 每個論點配一個數字、單位與日期，勝過三個形容詞。 - 每段做一次「那又怎樣」測試：如果它不能幫讀者決定或行動，就是裝飾。 - 精簡不等於無禮，短訊也可以客氣而完整。 匯報的表達方式 匯報只會被聽一次，所以結構要「聽得見」。 - 開場說目的與路線圖，正文不超過三個重點，用「首先、其次、最後」標示，結尾重複要求。 - 每張投影片一個訊息，注意力才會留在講者身上。 - 出聲排練計時，特別是開頭三十秒。 - 準備三條可能被問的問題與短答案。 - 望向觀眾而不是螢幕，轉折位停一停，把提問視為興趣而不是攻擊。 中英夾雜與專業術語 雙語工作環境經常轉換語言。語碼轉換本身正常，但要服務聽眾。 - 雙方都熟悉的英文術語可以保留；對外或對高層時改用中文；術語第一次出現時先定義。 - 一致性比純度重要：一個概念只用一個譯名，一份文件只用一種語域。 - 不要只因為某個字用另一種語言說得快就中途轉換；也要留意翻譯腔，因為它會削弱說服力。 渠道 最適合 結構 語氣 公函的固定部件 公函有讀者熟悉並會檢查的固定骨架。稱謂與發文者之後，依次是三個動作： - 主旨：用一行點題。 - 說明：交代背景與理由。 - 辦法：寫清楚應做甚麼、由誰做、何時做。 加上「謹啟」與日期即成。固定的開首與結語承載語域：「台鑒」「敬啟者」所表達的尊重，是電郵稱謂做不到的。記住一整套並重複使用；聊天式開首配正式結語，只會顯得粗心。 公函骨架 主旨 → 說明 → 辦法 預算、人手與應變 審批往往取決於實務部分：財政預算、人手與物資、應變措施。 - 預算用表格列出項目、數量、單價與總額，並解釋任何看似偏大的數字。 - 人手部分寫明誰在何時做甚麼——義工、講者、交通——讓審批者看見計劃有人執行，而不是空想。 - 應變部分預先寫出可能出錯的事（下雨、延誤、參加人數不足）與後備方案。 有務實應變的計劃書，比承諾「一切順利」的更專業。 資源檢查 人力 → 財力 → 物力 → 時間 由廣東話口語轉為書面語 書面語與廣東話口語在語法與詞彙上都不同。 - 助詞「咗、嘅、嚟」屬於口語，書面應寫成「了、的、來」。 - 句末語氣詞（呀、啦、囉）與中英夾雜的填充語，都不應出現在正式文件。 - 可靠方法是先寫意思，不要直接抄口語；一開始就用書面語起草，再出聲讀一遍，抓出漏入口語的地方。 - 若某句口語難以轉換，就圍繞動詞重寫整句：「搞掂」寫成「完成」，「傾」寫成「商討」，句子通常也會縮短。 口語轉書面 咗→了 · 嘅→的 · 嚟→來 · 搞掂→完成 · 傾→商討 語域 某個讀者與場合所期望的正式程度與詞彙層次。 語碼轉換 在對話或句子中轉用另一種語言，通常為了配合聽眾或題材。 路標語 口頭或書面提示，讓讀者知道論證的方向與段落數目。 摘要 開首的短段落，在細節之前交代要求、成本與效益。 名詞化 把動詞改成名詞片語，往往令句子變長、變得不直接。 公函 有固定結構的正式書信：主旨、說明、辦法，配以固定稱謂與結語。 書面語 中文的書面語域，在助詞、語法與詞彙上都與廣東話口語不同。 任何寫作題，第一行寫目的，最後一行寫行動與期限。 同一個要求準備一句正式寫法與一句口語寫法，並能解釋兩者差別。 匯報題目用「開場、三個路標重點、總結」的結構作答。 解釋語碼轉換時，說成「按聽眾決定」，而不是「中文不好」。 計劃書題目即使未有要求，也要寫預算與應變；評分者會找完整骨架。

subjects.title: Engineering Statistics
subjects.subtitle: Probability, estimation and decisions under uncertainty
subjects.summary: The language of uncertainty for engineers: describing a sample, choosing a distribution, putting a range around an estimate and testing a claim. It is the bridge between measurements and decisions on site.
subjects.text: The language of uncertainty for engineers: describing a sample, choosing a distribution, putting a range around an estimate and testing a claim. It is the bridge between measurements and decisions on site. Describing a sample Two features summarise most data: where it sits and how spread out it is. The mean is the balance point, the median resists outliers and the mode is the most frequent value. For spread, the sample standard deviation divides by n − 1 rather than n, correcting the tendency of a sample to understate variation in the population. Always plot before you summarise: a histogram shows skew, gaps and outliers that a mean cannot. - Comparing mean and median is a quick skew check. - The coefficient of variation, s divided by x̄, compares spread between variables measured on different scales. Sample mean x̄ = (1/n) Σ xi Sample standard deviation s = √[ Σ(xi − x̄)² / (n − 1) ] Probability and random variables Probability assigns a number between 0 and 1 to an event. The multiplication rule introduces conditional probability: P(A | B) is the probability of A given that B has happened. Events are independent when P(A | B) = P(A), and only then does the joint probability factorise as P(A) P(B). A random variable maps outcomes to numbers. Its expectation E(X) is the long-run average and its variance Var(X) measures spread around it. - Shifting a variable changes its mean but not its spread. - Scaling it multiplies the spread by the scale factor. Conditional probability P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B) Linear transformations E(aX + b) = a E(X) + b; Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X) The normal distribution The normal distribution N(μ, σ²) is symmetric and bell-shaped, fixed entirely by its mean and standard deviation. About 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two and 99.7% within three — the empirical rule, which makes quick plausibility checks possible. To use tables, standardise first, then find the tail area for the z value and combine tails for two-sided questions. Draw the curve, shade the area you want and label it before reading a table; sign and tail errors, not misunderstanding, cause most lost marks. Standard score z = (x − μ) / σ Binomial and Poisson The binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials with the same probability p: fixed n, two outcomes, constant p, independence. Its mean is np and its variance np(1 − p). The Poisson counts events in a fixed interval of time or space when they occur independently at a constant rate λ; its mean and variance are both λ. Poisson is the large-n, small-p limit of the binomial with λ = np, so it suits rare events such as defects per batch or calls per hour. - Check the assumptions first: no fixed number of trials rules out the binomial. - A strongly varying rate rules out the Poisson. Binomial probability P(X = x) = C(n, x) · p^x · (1 − p)^(n − x) Poisson probability P(X = x) = e^(−λ) · λ^x / x! Distribution What it models Parameters Mean Variance Sampling and the central limit theorem A statistic calculated from a sample is itself random: repeat the sampling and the mean changes. The sampling distribution of the mean has mean μ and standard error σ/√n, so quadrupling the sample halves the standard error. The central limit theorem says that for large n the sample mean is approximately normal whatever the population shape, which is why normal-based methods survive on skewed data. Roughly thirty observations is often enough, but heavy skew needs more. When σ is unknown, replace it with s and use the t distribution, whose heavier tails account for the extra uncertainty. Standard error of the mean SE = σ / √n Confidence intervals A confidence interval puts a range around an estimate and states the uncertainty. With σ known the interval is x̄ ± z σ/√n; with σ unknown use s and the t critical value with n − 1 degrees of freedom. A 95% interval is wider than a 90% one, and it narrows as n grows. subjects.subtitle: Cleaning, plotting and modelling real data
subjects.summary: R turns a spreadsheet of measurements into a defensible argument: tidy the data, describe it, plot it, fit it and forecast it. Most of the skill lies in the order of those steps and in scripts that someone else can re-run.
subjects.text: R turns a spreadsheet of measurements into a defensible argument: tidy the data, describe it, plot it, fit it and forecast it. Most of the skill lies in the order of those steps and in scripts that someone else can re-run. Start with the data frame A data frame is the unit of work: each row is one observation and each column is one variable. R keeps columns as vectors, so measurements stay numeric while categories should be factors. read.csv() only reads the file; then check the shape with str() and head(). Tidy data means one row per case, one column per variable and one value per cell. Most later trouble — numbers imported as text, dates stored as characters — is visible here, and fixing it early is cheaper than patching a model. Describe before modelling. summary() gives range, quartiles and missing counts; mean(), median(), sd() and IQR() give the numbers you will quote. A mean far from the median hints at skew or a stray observation. Read, inspect, describe pm <- read.csv('data/pm.csv') str(pm); dim(pm); head(pm) summary(pm$value); sd(pm$value, na.rm = TRUE) Wrangle with verbs, not loops Wrangling is a sequence of small verbs, each doing one thing: - filter() keeps rows - select() keeps columns - mutate() adds a column - arrange() sorts - groupby() with summarise() gives one summary row per group The pipe | passes each result into the next step, so the code reads in reasoning order. If a step is hard to name, it is doing two jobs and should be split. groupby() with summarise() also replaces most hand-written loops over categories. A small grouped pipeline daily <- pm | filter(!is.na(value)) | mutate(month = format(date, '%m')) | groupby(month) | summarise(meanpm = mean(value), n = n()) Task Tool Watch for Hunt missing values and outliers Missing values are not neutral: they shrink the sample and bias a mean if they cluster in one period or one site. Count them with mean(is.na(x)), then decide to drop, impute or model them — and write the decision down. Outliers need a decision too. A reading twenty times the others may be a real event or a typing error, and the two deserve different treatment. A boxplot shows the shape; a log scale sometimes tames a long tail. Share of missing values mean(is.na(x)) Plots are arguments about data The grammar of graphics splits a plot into data, an aesthetic mapping and a geometry. In ggplot(), aes() says which variable controls x, y, colour or shape, and the geom says what is drawn. Changing the geometry changes the claim. Colour should encode a variable, not decorate. facetwrap() makes small multiples, often clearer than five layered lines. Label both axes and give the title the takeaway; ggsave() keeps the figure reproducible. Points with a mapped colour ggplot(pm, aes(x = date, y = value, colour = site)) + geompoint() + labs(x = 'Date', y = 'PM2.5 (µg/m³)') Regression: a fitted line, not a law lm(y ~ x, data = pm) fits the least-squares line. The slope is the expected change in y per one-unit change in x, so its units matter and its sign must make physical sense. R² is the share of variance in y explained by the model, not the probability that it is correct. Always inspect residuals: a curve means the relationship is not linear, a fan shape means the variance changes, and a few extreme points may dominate the fit. Correlation is not causation, and extrapolation beyond the observed range is not evidence. Simple linear model y = β₀ + β₁ x + ε Coefficient of determination R² = 1 − SSE / SST Time series, seasonality and ARIMA A time series is ordered, so neighbouring values are related and ordinary regression assumptions fail. Convert with ts(x, frequency = 12) for monthly data, then plot it: trend, repeating seasonality and noise should be visible. decompose() splits the series into those parts. A series is stationary when its mean, variance and autocorrelation do not drift with time. Differencing removes a trend; the autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation plots then suggest the order

subjects.title: Fluid Mechanics
subjects.subtitle: Pressure, flow and forces on bodies in water
subjects.summary: How fluids at rest and in motion push on structures, and how water moves through pipes, channels and machines. Hydrostatics, buoyancy, Bernoulli, momentum, friction losses and boundary layers form one connected toolkit for water engineering.
subjects.text: How fluids at rest and in motion push on structures, and how water moves through pipes, channels and machines. Hydrostatics, buoyancy, Bernoulli, momentum, friction losses and boundary layers form one connected toolkit for water engineering. What makes a fluid a fluid A fluid deforms continuously under shear, however small the shear. Two properties dominate: density ρ, the mass per unit volume, and dynamic viscosity μ, the resistance to shearing. For a Newtonian fluid the shear stress is proportional to the velocity gradient, with μ as the constant. Water near room temperature has ρ ≈ 998 kg/m³ and μ ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa·s; air is about 1.2 kg/m³ and 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ Pa·s. Kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ is convenient because it appears directly in the Reynolds number. A real fluid sticks to a solid surface — the no-slip condition — so velocity is zero at the wall. That one fact creates the boundary layer and most of the friction in engineering. Newtonian shear stress τ = μ · du/dy Kinematic viscosity ν = μ / ρ Pressure in a fluid at rest Pressure acts equally in all directions in a fluid at rest, and depth sets its value: p = p₀ + ρ g h below a free surface. The same fluid at the same depth has the same pressure whatever the container's shape. A manometer reads a pressure difference as a column height, and pressure head p/(ρg), quoted in metres of water, keeps the arithmetic in the same units as elevation. A hydraulic jack uses the same principle: modest pressure over a small piston, multiplied by a much larger area. Hydrostatic pressure p = p₀ + ρ g h Forces on submerged surfaces The force on a plane surface is the pressure at its centroid times its area: F = ρ g h̄ A, where h̄ is the depth of the centroid. On a horizontal base this is pressure times area; on a vertical gate the pressure grows with depth, so the resultant acts lower. That point is the centre of pressure, ycp = yc + Ix/(yc A), with y measured along the plane from the free surface. For a rectangular gate of depth d and width b, Ix = b d³/12. Keep the dry side in the balance. A gate with water on one side and air on the other feels a net force, and that difference is what the hinge must resist. Force on a plane surface F = ρ g h̄ A Centre of pressure ycp = yc + Ix / (yc A) Buoyancy and floating stability Archimedes: the buoyant force equals the weight of fluid displaced, FB = ρfluid g Vdisplaced, acting through the centroid of the displaced volume. A body denser than the fluid sinks until the displaced weight balances it; a floating body displaces exactly its own weight. Floating upright is a separate question. When the body tilts, the centre of buoyancy moves and the weight and buoyancy forces form a couple. The metacentric height GM measures that restoring effect: positive is stable, negative capsizes. Wide, shallow hulls are stable; narrow, tall ones are not. Buoyant force FB = ρfluid g Vdisplaced Continuity and the energy equation Mass is conserved. For steady, incompressible flow through a changing area, Q = A₁V₁ = A₂V₂, so a constriction speeds the fluid up and a wider section slows it down. Bernoulli's equation relates pressure, velocity and elevation along a streamline for steady, frictionless flow: p/(ρg) + V²/(2g) + z = constant. Each term is a head in metres — pressure, velocity and elevation head. It explains the venturi meter (higher throat velocity, lower pressure) and the pitot tube, which turns velocity head into a pressure difference. It fails wherever losses or pumps matter, which is most real pipework. Continuity Q = A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ Bernoulli equation p/(ρg) + V²/(2g) + z = constant Momentum and forces on bodies Bernoulli gives pressures; momentum gives forces. For a steady stream, the net force on the fluid equals its rate of change of momentum, ΣF = ρQ(Vout − Vin), treated as vectors. The same force acts in reverse on whatever turns the flow — a bend, reducer or vane. A jet on a plate is the standard case: a flat plate stopping the jet normally feels F = ρQV,

subjects.subtitle: Effective stress, consolidation, shear strength and earth pressure
subjects.summary: Soil is a three-phase material whose strength and settlement depend on effective stress, drainage and stress history. This page connects the phase relationships, classification tests, consolidation theory and shear strength that underpin foundation and slope design.
subjects.text: Soil is a three-phase material whose strength and settlement depend on effective stress, drainage and stress history. This page connects the phase relationships, classification tests, consolidation theory and shear strength that underpin foundation and slope design. The three-phase picture Soil is a skeleton of particles with water and air in the gaps. The void volume is Vv = Vw + Va, and the phase relationships compare those volumes and weights. - Void ratio e = Vv/Vs measures looseness; porosity n = e/(1+e) is the same idea as a volume fraction. - Water content w = Ww/Ws compares water mass with solid mass, and degree of saturation Sr = Vw/Vv says how full the voids are. - Specific gravity Gs is about 2.65 for quartz particles. - The unit weights follow from the phase diagram: bulk γ = (Gs + e Sr) γw/(1+e) and dry γd = γ/(1+w) = Gs γw/(1+e). Consistency saves later errors. Void ratio e = Vv / Vs Dry unit weight γd = Gs γw / (1 + e) Classification and Atterberg limits Coarse soils are classified by sieve analysis and fine soils by the hydrometer test. The grading curve gives D₁₀, D₃₀ and D₆₀, and the uniformity coefficient Cu = D₆₀/D₁₀: a high value means a well-graded soil. For fine soils the Atterberg limits mark the water contents where behaviour changes. - The liquid limit LL is where the soil stops flowing (20 mm cone penetration in the fall-cone test). - The plastic limit PL is where a 3 mm thread crumbles. - The plasticity index PI = LL − PL measures the range of plastic behaviour. A high PI signals a compressible clay, and a plasticity chart separates silts from clays. Plasticity index PI = LL − PL Uniformity coefficient Cu = D₆₀ / D₁₀ Compaction Compaction densifies soil by expelling air, usually with rollers. The laboratory Proctor test compacts a sample at several water contents and plots dry density against water content, giving a curve that peaks at the optimum moisture content. Too dry and particles lock against each other; too wet and water occupies the voids the soil would otherwise fill. Compaction raises strength and bearing capacity and reduces settlement and permeability, which is why fill is placed in thin layers and compacted to a specified relative compaction rather than simply dumped. Relative compaction RC = γd(field) / γd(max, lab) Effective stress and seepage Strength and settlement are governed by effective stress: σ' = σ − u, where σ is the total stress from the weight of soil and water above and u is the pore water pressure. Same total stress and different pore pressure give completely different behaviour. - Below the water table, u = ρw g h and effective stress uses the submerged unit weight γ' = γsat − γw. - Above it, capillary water can give negative pore pressure and temporarily raise σ'. - Seepage adds a force. Darcy's law gives v = k i and q = k i A, with gradient i = Δh/L. - When upward seepage approaches the submerged weight, effective stress reaches zero: the critical hydraulic gradient is ic = (Gs − 1)/(1 + e), and beyond it the soil boils and piping can begin. Effective stress σ' = σ − u Darcy's law v = k i Critical hydraulic gradient ic = (Gs − 1) / (1 + e) Consolidation and settlement Consolidation is the time-dependent compression of a saturated clay as excess pore water pressure dissipates. The load is carried by water at first; as it drains, the pressure transfers to the soil skeleton and the void ratio falls, producing settlement. The oedometer test loads a sample in increments and plots void ratio against log pressure. The slope of the virgin compression line is the compression index Cc, and the preconsolidation pressure marks the largest stress ever carried. The overconsolidation ratio OCR compares that stress with the present one; an overconsolidated clay settles much less. Settlement follows sc = Cc H/(1 + e₀) · log₁₀((σ'₀ + Δσ)/σ'₀), and the rate depends on the coefficient of consolidation cv. One-dimensional settlement sc = [Cc H / (1 + e₀)] · log₁₀[(σ'₀ + Δσ) / σ'₀] Shear

subjects.summary: How positions and heights are measured, computed and set out on site: levelling, traverse adjustment, coordinates, total stations, GNSS and curves. It is the subject that turns ground observations into numbers you can build from.
subjects.text: How positions and heights are measured, computed and set out on site: levelling, traverse adjustment, coordinates, total stations, GNSS and curves. It is the subject that turns ground observations into numbers you can build from. Control first, then detail Every survey fixes new points relative to points already known. The known ones form the control; everything else is detail. Control is denser and more accurate than the work hanging off it, because every later measurement inherits its error. The working rule is whole to part: build the frame — horizontal stations with coordinates, benchmarks with reduced levels — then fill in detail from that frame. Coordinates need an origin and heights need a datum, so both must be stated. A survey that starts from detail and works upwards has no way to check itself. Accuracy is how close a result is to the truth; precision is how repeatable it is. A tight cluster of readings away from the truth is precise but biased. Levelling: the book must balance Levelling measures height differences. Set the instrument between two staffs; its line of sight defines a height of collimation. The first reading after a setup is a back sight onto a point of known level; intermediate sights locate points between changes; a fore sight is the last reading before the instrument moves. The staff then stays as a change point, so it must sit on something stable. Two booking conventions dominate: - Height of collimation method: add the back sight to the known level once, then subtract every other reading from that height. - Rise and fall method: compares consecutive readings and is slower, but it checks every intermediate sight. Balance back and fore sight distances to cancel collimation and curvature, keep sights short, and avoid readings below about half a metre. Height of collimation HI = RL + BS Rise and fall rise = BS − FS Angles, bearings and the whole-circle convention Directions are measured clockwise from north. A whole-circle bearing runs from 0° to 360°; a reduced bearing quotes the same direction from north or south towards east or west. Turning a sight line clockwise from the back station to the forward station gives an angle to the right, the convention most data loggers expect. Angles in a closed polygon form a fixed sum, so the gap between measured and theoretical sum is an angular misclosure. Interior angles of an n-sided figure add to (n − 2) × 180°. Carrying bearings onward is bookkeeping: take the back bearing of the previous leg (forward bearing ± 180°), add the angle to the right, and subtract 360° if needed. Interior angle sum Σθ = (n − 2) × 180° Bearing transfer WCBnext = WCBback + θright Traverse computation in a fixed order A traverse measures angles and distances along a chain of stations. Compute in sequence: - adjust the angles - carry bearings through the figure - convert each leg into north and east components called latitude and departure - add them to test closure - distribute the remainder Angular misclosure is spread equally over the angles because each was observed with equal effort. The vector sum of the coordinate errors is the linear misclosure, and its size relative to total length is the relative precision. The Bowditch (compass) rule shares coordinate corrections in proportion to leg length, so short legs move little. That weighting suits comparable angular and distance error; stronger distances call for another weighting. Angular misclosure eθ = Σθmeasured − (n − 2) × 180° Latitude and departure ΔN = d · cos θ, ΔE = d · sin θ Bowditch correction C = −e · di / Σd Choosing a field method Different tasks ask for different geometry. Radiation is quick when one station sees everything; intersection needs no occupation of the target; a traverse builds new control; GNSS suits open ground but dislikes canopy and reflection.
