subjects.subtitle: Plans, quality, prefabrication and professional practice
subjects.summary: How projects are organised so that what is built matches what was specified: quality systems, inspection plans, non-conformance, prefabrication, model coordination and handover. It is the professional layer that holds the technical work together.
subjects.text: How projects are organised so that what is built matches what was specified: quality systems, inspection plans, non-conformance, prefabrication, model coordination and handover. It is the professional layer that holds the technical work together. Quality is planned, not inspected in A quality management system is the set of responsibilities, procedures and records that make quality repeatable rather than accidental. It runs on a process loop: agree what is required, plan how it will be achieved, do the work, check the result against the specification, and act on the gap. - Quality assurance is prevention — method statements, mock-ups, training, supplier assessment, design checks. - Quality control is detection — inspection, testing and measurement against acceptance criteria. - A project leaning entirely on control is paying to find its own mistakes. - The cost of quality is how that trade-off becomes visible. The inspection and test plan An inspection and test plan (ITP) lists, for each activity, what is checked, against which acceptance criterion, by whom, at what frequency, and what record proves it happened. It is written before work starts and follows the construction sequence, so it doubles as a quality programme. - Hold points: work cannot continue until the inspection is passed and signed. - Witness points: the inspector is invited but the work may proceed. - Writing an ITP is an exercise in risk: hold the points that would be expensive or unsafe to discover late, and witness the rest. Inspection, testing and non-conformance Inspection follows the work: receiving inspection on delivered material, in-process inspection during construction, and final inspection before handover. Testing may be destructive (cubes, cores) or non-destructive (covermeter, rebound hammer, ultrasonic, half-cell potential), and a result means little without its method and sampling plan. When something fails, the response is a non-conformance report: - contain the item - record the facts - agree a disposition (rework, repair, accept by concession, or reject) - find the root cause - close the corrective action Treating each report as an isolated complaint hides the pattern; grouping them by trade or location is where the improvement sits. The seven basic quality tools Seven simple tools do most of the analysis a quality engineer needs. - Check sheet collects counts as events happen. - Histogram shows the spread of a measurement. - Pareto chart ranks defect causes by frequency so the vital few are tackled first. - Cause-and-effect diagram traces an effect back through materials, methods, people, plant and environment. - Scatter diagram tests whether two variables move together. - Control chart separates common-cause variation from special causes over time. - Flow chart maps the process so it can be improved. The tools are cheap because they run on honesty: they only work when data is collected at the point of work, labelled with the process that produced it, and then acted on. A Pareto chart of defects that nobody categorised is a picture, not a decision. Tool Question it answers Process capability and control limits A process in control is not automatically capable. Control limits describe what the process is doing; specification limits describe what the customer will accept. Plotting sample means against control limits reveals drift and special causes, while capability indices compare the natural spread with the tolerance. - Cp asks whether the spread fits the tolerance at all. - Cpk also asks whether the process is centred. - A Cp above 1.33 with a Cpk near 0.6 means the process is consistent but badly aimed — adjust the setting, not the inspection frequency. Sampling plans then decide how many items to test for the confidence required, which is why acceptance criteria always pair a method with a sampling rate. Process capability Cp = (USL − LSL) / (6σ) Centred capability Cpk = min[(USL − μ)/(3σ), (μ − LSL)/(3σ)] Control limits for sample means

subjects.subtitle: Frames, influence lines, stiffness and the behaviour of real structures
subjects.summary: How the forces and deflections of real frames are found: determinacy, virtual work, influence lines, moment distribution and stiffness methods. It turns a sketch of a structure into numbers an engineer can defend.
subjects.text: How the forces and deflections of real frames are found: determinacy, virtual work, influence lines, moment distribution and stiffness methods. It turns a sketch of a structure into numbers an engineer can defend. Determinacy and stability Equilibrium supplies three independent equations for each planar free body. Count the members, joints and reaction components: for a rigid-jointed frame the degree of static indeterminacy is Ds = 3m + r − 3j. - Ds = 0: reactions follow from equilibrium. - Ds 0: that many redundants remain. - Ds < 0: warns of a mechanism. - Internal hinges reduce the count. Determinacy is arithmetic, not proof of stability. Parallel supports, or reactions meeting at one point, can leave a determinate structure free to move, so sketch the mechanism first. Degree of static indeterminacy, planar frame Ds = 3m + r − 3j Virtual work and the unit load method The unit load method finds one displacement at a time. Apply a virtual unit load at the point and in the direction required, determine the internal virtual forces, then sum the products of virtual and real actions over the structure. - For a frame: Σ∫ M m / (EI) ds. - For a truss: Σ n N L / (A E). The sign follows the assumed virtual direction: a negative result means the displacement is opposite to the unit load. It is ideal for checking a computer result at a chosen point. Unit load method, frame Δ = Σ∫ M m / (E I) ds Unit load method, truss Δ = Σ n N L / (A E) The flexibility method The flexibility (force) method handles indeterminate structures by removing supports or internal actions until a statically determinate released structure remains. The unknowns are the redundant forces X; the price of release is that the released structure must be made to behave like the real one. Compatibility supplies the missing equations: the displacement at each released coordinate, caused by the applied loads plus the redundants, must equal its real value — usually zero. In matrix form f X + D = 0, where fij is the displacement at coordinate i from a unit redundant at j and D is the displacement there from the loads alone. Each coefficient follows from virtual work. When using diagram multiplication, split the moment diagrams into simple shapes whose areas and centroids are known. The slope of a bending moment diagram equals the shear, so a diagram whose slope changes at a joint must be decomposed — a parabola and a triangle, not one imagined shape. Compatibility equations in matrix form f X + D = 0 Flexibility coefficient fij = Σ∫ mi mj / (E I) ds Influence lines An influence line shows how one response — reaction, shear, moment or deflection — varies as a unit load travels across the structure. Once the line is known, any load train is handled by superposition: multiply each load by the ordinate beneath it and add. Placing loads over the largest ordinates gives the governing position, which is why they suit bridges and crane girders. The Müller-Breslau principle gives the shape directly: release the structure at the point of interest, impose a unit displacement or rotation in the direction of the response, and the resulting deflected shape is the influence line. For a simply supported beam, the moment influence line has an ordinate a b / L beneath the section. Moment influence ordinate, simply supported beam y = a b / L Moment distribution Moment distribution solves indeterminate beams and frames joint by joint, without simultaneous equations. Lock every joint, write the fixed-end moments from the member loads, then release one joint at a time. The unbalanced moment is shared between the members in proportion to their stiffness, and part is carried over to fixed far ends; repeat until the carry-over is negligible. - For constant EI, stiffness is 4EI/L when the far end is fixed and 3EI/L when it is pinned. - The carry-over factor is 0.5 to a fixed end and zero to a pinned end. subjects.summary: How a construction project is planned, procured, programmed and controlled: work breakdown, critical path, cost and earned value, site records, BIM coordination and safety. The management layer that turns drawings into a delivered building.
subjects.text: How a construction project is planned, procured, programmed and controlled: work breakdown, critical path, cost and earned value, site records, BIM coordination and safety. The management layer that turns drawings into a delivered building. The project as a system A construction project is a temporary organisation assembled to deliver a defined scope within time, cost and quality constraints. Scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, resources and stakeholders are interdependent: a change in one moves the others, and the cost of absorbing a change rises sharply as the project advances. Integration means keeping those trade-offs visible and decided, not letting each discipline optimise alone. The client's brief is the reference point: a clear statement of what is required, what is excluded and how success will be measured prevents most later disputes. Work breakdown and programming Programming starts with a work breakdown structure: the scope is divided into packages, each package becomes activities, and the activities are linked by logic and given durations and resources. - A network shows the logic; a Gantt chart shows the same programme against a calendar and communicates it better. - The programme is a forecast, not a record, so it is updated as work and information change. - Resource levelling flattens peaks that cannot be staffed. - Crashing adds resources to shorten the critical path, usually at extra cost. - Both change the risk profile and should never be done silently. Critical path and float The critical path is the longest path through the network and therefore sets the project duration. A forward pass gives earliest start and finish; a backward pass gives latest start and finish. - Total float is the amount an activity can slip without delaying completion; activities with zero float are critical. - Float belongs to the project, not one trade. Using it early removes the buffer that could absorb a later delay, so float is not necessarily spare time. - Free float is the smaller amount that can be used without affecting the next activity's earliest start. Earliest finish EF = ES + duration Total float TF = LS − ES = LF − EF Crashing and the cost–time trade Crashing shortens an activity by spending money: more crews, more plant, longer shifts or a faster method. It only helps if the activity sits on the critical path; spending on an activity with float buys nothing. The cost slope prices the trade — the extra cost per day saved — and the cheapest slopes are crashed first. Slopes rise as an activity is compressed, because the easy savings run out. Beyond a limit the activity cannot be shortened at all, and quality and safety deteriorate under rush. Crashing is therefore a ranked list of slopes, not a single decision, and the network must be recomputed after each step. Cost slope CS = (Cc − Cn) / (tn − tc) Procurement and contracts Procurement decides who designs, who builds and who carries which risk. - Traditional design-bid-build: the client holds the design. - Design and build: one organisation holds both design and build. - Management contracting: brings the builder in early and awards packages as design develops. - Each route trades cost certainty against speed, flexibility and the client's exposure to change. The contract must match the route: lump sum, remeasurement or cost-plus, with clear provisions for variations, delay and payment. Most disputes trace back to a mismatch between route, contract and expectation. Route Design responsibility Cost certainty at award Best when Contract administration: variations and claims Contracts change after award. A variation is an instructed change to the work: an addition, a deletion, a different material or a changed sequence. The machinery matters as much as the change — who may instruct, how it is valued, and what happens if the parties disagree. Claims arise where one party believes the other's act or a risk event has cost it time or money. The entitlement test is disciplined

subjects.subtitle: Limit state design, section capacity and connection checks
subjects.summary: How steel members and connections are checked at the ultimate and serviceability limit states: classification, bending, shear, buckling, welds and bolts. It is where a section table, a design code and a calculator meet.
subjects.text: How steel members and connections are checked at the ultimate and serviceability limit states: classification, bending, shear, buckling, welds and bolts. It is where a section table, a design code and a calculator meet. Two numbers and a factor of safety Limit state design compares a factored load effect with a factored resistance and requires the resistance to be the larger: Ed ≤ Rd. - Load factors cover uncertainty of dead, imposed and wind loads; material factors cover yield strength and fabrication. - Ultimate limit states cover strength, stability and fire; serviceability limit states cover deflection, vibration and durability. - The aim is a small, known probability of failure during the design life, not zero risk. - Ductility and robustness matter: a structure that warns before it fails is safer. Limit state check Ed ≤ Rd Steel, strength and slenderness Steel is specified by grade — S275, S355, S460 — where the number is the minimum yield strength in N/mm² for that thickness. The design strength used in calculations is py = fy / γM. - Steel is stiff, strong and ductile; ductility allows redistribution of force and gives visible warning before fracture. - Residual stresses from rolling and welding do not reduce the squash load, but they do reduce stiffness and bring buckling forward. - Toughness matters in thick sections and at low temperature, so the impact sub-grade belongs in the specification. Design strength py = fy / γM Section classification Local buckling depends on how slender each plate element is. The width-to-thickness ratio b/T is compared with limits written as multiples of ε, where ε = √(275/py) and 275 N/mm² is the reference yield strength. - Class 1 plastic: can form a plastic hinge and rotate. - Class 2 compact: reaches the plastic moment with little rotation. - Class 3 semi-compact: reaches yield at the extreme fibre only. - Class 4 slender: buckles locally before yield. - The whole section takes the worst class of its elements. Slenderness factor ε = √(275 / py) Class Local behaviour Bending resistance Tension members: gross, net and effective area Tension is the cleanest steel check — no buckling, just area times strength — but the detailing is subtle. The gross area Ag is the full cross-section; the net area An removes bolt holes; and the effective area Ae reduces further for shear lag: when bolts connect only one leg of an angle, the outstand leg joins the load gradually through the corner rather than at the connection. - Single angle bolted through one leg: An = Ag − 0.3 a₂, where a₂ is the area of the unconnected leg. - Double angle sharing the connection: An = Ag − 0.15 a₂. - Effective area: Ae = Ke An, with Ke of about 1.1 for S355 steel. - A tension test on 65 × 65 angles showed strain falling steeply across the outstand leg — shear lag made visible. Net area, single angle bolted through one leg An = Ag − 0.3 a₂ Net area, double angle An = Ag − 0.15 a₂ Effective area Ae = Ke An Bending and shear The bending resistance of a Class 1 or 2 section is the plastic moment Mc = py S, where S is the plastic section modulus. A Class 3 section uses the elastic modulus Z instead, and a Class 4 section uses the effective modulus. - Shear is carried mainly by the web: Vc = 0.6 py Av, where Av is the shear area. - When the shear force exceeds about 60% of the shear resistance, the moment capacity must be reduced for the shear area lost. - Concentrated loads also require web bearing and web buckling checks, with stiffeners where the web is too thin. - Deflection is a separate serviceability check with unfactored loads. subjects.summary: How engineers draw conclusions from limited data: sampling, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, designed experiments and regression. It is the discipline that keeps a decision honest when the measurements are noisy.
subjects.text: How engineers draw conclusions from limited data: sampling, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, designed experiments and regression. It is the discipline that keeps a decision honest when the measurements are noisy. Variation is the data Measurements vary, even when the thing measured does not. Engineering data therefore needs a centre and a spread: the sample mean estimates the population mean, and the sample standard deviation estimates the typical distance of a reading from that mean. - The coefficient of variation, CV = s / x̄, compares variability between datasets with different units or means. - Always report the sample size and the units with the summary. - A mean without a spread hides the risk, and a spread without a mean has no scale; the pair is the minimum honest description of a dataset. Sample mean x̄ = Σx / n Sample standard deviation s = √[Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1)] Coefficient of variation CV = s / x̄ Sampling and the central limit theorem A sample is useful only if it represents the population. Random selection, independence and a consistent measurement method are the assumptions that make inference valid; a biased sample cannot be rescued by a larger n. - The standard error of the mean is SE = s / √n, which shrinks as the square root of the sample size. - The central limit theorem says that the distribution of the sample mean approaches normal as n grows, whatever the shape of the population. - This is why the t and z procedures work for means of moderately large samples even when the data are not normal. Standard error of the mean SE = s / √n Confidence intervals A confidence interval puts a range around an estimate. For a mean with an unknown population standard deviation, the interval is x̄ ± t s / √n, where t comes from the t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom. The width grows with the confidence level and the variability, and falls with the sample size. The interpretation is easy to get wrong. A 95% interval does not mean there is a 95% probability that μ lies inside this particular interval; it means that 95% of intervals built this way would contain μ. The interval estimates the parameter, not the individual readings. Confidence interval for a mean x̄ ± t s / √n Hypothesis tests A hypothesis test asks whether the data are consistent with a stated value. Set a null hypothesis H0 (no effect, no difference) and an alternative H1, choose a significance level α, and calculate a test statistic. For a mean, t = (x̄ − μ0) / (s / √n). - The p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme as the observed one, assuming H0 is true; reject H0 when p < α. - A Type I error rejects a true null; a Type II error fails to reject a false one. - Statistical significance is not practical importance: a tiny, precise difference can be significant and still irrelevant. One-sample t statistic t = (x̄ − μ0) / (s / √n) Comparing two populations Two designs, two suppliers or two curing methods are compared by their means. - For independent samples with similar variances, pool the standard deviations and use a two-sample t test; the degrees of freedom are n1 + n2 − 2. - For paired observations — the same specimen before and after, or matched pairs — test the differences instead, which removes the between-pair variability. - Report the estimated difference with a confidence interval, not just a p-value. - A significant difference of 0.2 MPa may be real but too small to change a specification; the interval shows both the size and the precision of the effect. Pooled variance sp² = [(n1 − 1)s1² + (n2 − 1)s2²] / (n1 + n2 − 2) Two-sample t statistic t = (x̄1 − x̄2) / [sp √(1/n1 + 1/n2)] ANOVA and designed experiments To compare three or more means, use analysis of variance rather than repeated t tests, which would inflate the chance of a false positive. subjects.summary: Learning from mobility data: regression for speeds, classification for road signs, and neural networks that must generalise. The page covers the training loop, honest evaluation, and the privacy questions that come with location records.
subjects.text: Learning from mobility data: regression for speeds, classification for road signs, and neural networks that must generalise. The page covers the training loop, honest evaluation, and the privacy questions that come with location records. What a mobility model predicts Smart mobility turns sensor records into forecasts: link speed in fifteen minutes, the class of a road sign in a camera frame, the path a pedestrian will take next. The first decision is the task type, because it fixes the labels, the loss function and the evaluation. - Supervised learning: every example pairs a feature vector x with a known target y. - Regression: predicts a number. - Classification: predicts a category. - Unsupervised methods find structure without targets, such as clustering similar journeys. Regression: fitting a line to movement A linear model predicts a target as a weighted sum of inputs, ŷ = w · x + b. Training chooses weights that make predictions close to the observed values, usually by minimising the mean squared error. Squaring punishes large misses hardest — sensible for speed forecasts, where wild errors matter most. The loss is a surface in weight space. Gradient descent steps downhill, using the derivative for direction and a learning rate for step size. Linear regression model ŷ = w · x + b Mean squared error MSE = (1/n) Σ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)² Gradient descent update w ← w − η ∂L/∂w Classification, labels and the split A classifier outputs a score for each class, converted into a probability by a sigmoid for two classes or a softmax across several. The predicted label is the highest score, and the surface where two scores tie is the decision boundary. Before any tuning, hold back a test set that the model never sees. A model scored on its own training rows is only being checked for memory. For small datasets, cross-validation rotates the holdout so that every row is tested once. Overfitting is the default failure Training loss almost always falls as capacity grows; validation loss is the honest signal. When validation loss bottoms out and then rises while training loss keeps falling, the model has begun to fit noise. That gap is overfitting; a model too simple for the pattern is underfitting, and both losses stay high. Controls include: - fewer features or layers - regularisation that penalises large weights - augmentation that enlarges the effective dataset - early stopping at the validation minimum Regularised loss L = loss + λ Σ wᵢ² Neural networks: stacked transformations A neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs, adds a bias and passes the result through a non-linear activation such as ReLU. Stacking layers lets the network build its own features: early layers detect simple patterns, later ones combine them. Backpropagation applies the chain rule to find how each weight affected the loss, and an optimiser updates all weights together. Mini-batches trade noisy gradients for speed, and one pass over the data is an epoch. Without non-linearity, stacked linear layers collapse into one linear map. Neuron output a = f(W x + b) Convolutional networks for road signs A camera image is a grid of pixels, and flattening it destroys neighbourhood structure. A convolutional layer slides small learnable filters across the image, sharing weights at every position, so an edge detector learnt in one corner works in every corner. Pooling compresses the feature map and adds tolerance to small shifts. Road-sign datasets are often small and imbalanced, so transfer learning is standard: - start from a network trained on a large image collection - freeze the early layers - retrain the final layer for the sign classes Augmentation — rotation, brightness and crop — widens the training set. Convolution output size nout = (nin − k + 2p) / s + 1 Evaluation that matches the decision Accuracy misleads when classes are imbalanced: a detector that never predicts the rare give-way sign can still score 95%. subjects.summary: Writing and speaking for engineering practice: reports, executive summaries, emails and presentations that a busy reader can act on. It is the difference between work that is done and work that is understood.
subjects.text: Writing and speaking for engineering practice: reports, executive summaries, emails and presentations that a busy reader can act on. It is the difference between work that is done and work that is understood. Write for the reader's job A professional document exists to change what a reader knows or does. Before drafting, answer three questions: who is reading, what they need to decide or do, and what the one main message is. Write the purpose in the first two lines, keep one idea per paragraph, and lead each paragraph with its point rather than its background. A busy reader should not have to reconstruct your logic. The reader's job is the test: - A checking engineer needs the calculation and its assumptions. - A client needs the outcome, the cost and the decision required. Planning frame Purpose → Audience → Action → Tone The shape of a technical report Reports follow a predictable order because readers use them differently. A common spine is context and objective, method, evidence, interpretation, and conclusions with recommendations. - The introduction says why the work was done and what it covers. - The method is repeatable. - Findings come before explanation. - Recommendations are specific and assigned. Signposting helps: headings, numbering and a short opening sentence in each section tell the reader what the section does. Appendices hold raw data and long calculations so that the body stays readable. Report spine Context → Method → Evidence → Interpretation → Action Executive summaries earn the meeting Many readers will read the executive summary first, and some will read only it. It should stand alone: purpose, what was done, the main findings, and the recommendation, in roughly a tenth of the report's length. Write it last, when findings are settled, and add no information not in the report. Use concrete numbers and plain verbs. A summary that says testing indicated a potential concern hides the finding; one that says three of nine samples failed the strength requirement lets the reader act. Summary length Lsummary ≈ Lreport / 10 Email that gets a reply An email is a request with context. The subject line names the project and the action. Open with the purpose, give the minimum context, state what you need and by when, and close with a clear next step. Tone follows the relationship, the topic and the context: directness, formality and politeness are separate dials, not one switch. Cut wordy phrases: “due to the fact that” becomes “because”; “in order to” becomes “to”. Prefer the active voice and concrete verbs, and keep one register. Wordy Concise Presenting technical work Slides support a talk; they are not the talk. Put one message on each slide and make the title a claim the audience can read in three seconds, such as “drainage capacity fails at peak flow”. Show the chart, not a table of every number, and remove decoration that competes with the evidence. Signpost the argument: what the problem is, what you found, what it means, what you recommend. Rehearse to time, prepare one sentence for each likely question, and answer the question asked before adding context. In discussion, restate the question so the room hears it, answer briefly, then stop. Editing for concision Concise writing is not short writing; it is writing where every word carries weight. - Turn nominalisations back into verbs — “we investigated” rather than “an investigation was carried out”. - Cut redundant pairs such as “advance planning” or “true facts”. - Keep bullets parallel so they can be compared line by line. Read the draft aloud. Long sentences, missing verbs and repeated points reveal themselves to the ear. Then proofread for agreement, articles and consistent terminology; one wrong unit or figure costs more credibility than a slightly plain style. subjects.summary: Choosing a data structure is a decision about cost. This page covers arrays, lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, trees and graphs, then sorting, searching and the Big-O language used to compare them.
subjects.text: Choosing a data structure is a decision about cost. This page covers arrays, lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, trees and graphs, then sorting, searching and the Big-O language used to compare them. The structure is part of the algorithm An abstract data type is a contract: the operations and their meaning, with no promise about implementation. A data structure is one way to keep that contract, and every implementation trades something — time for memory, or generality for speed. - Finding whether a value exists: linear scan in an unsorted array, logarithmic search in a sorted one, average constant-time lookup in a hash table. - Name the operations the program performs most often before writing code. Arrays and linked lists An array stores elements in contiguous memory, so indexing is constant-time arithmetic, but inserting in the middle shifts everything after it. A linked list stores nodes that point to each other: inserting at a known node is constant-time, yet reaching position k means walking k nodes, and each step may miss the cache. - Use arrays for indexed reading and iteration; lists for splicing and reordering without random access. - A dynamic array amortises growth by doubling capacity, which makes appending O(1) on average. Stacks and queues A stack is last-in, first-out: push and pop at one end. It models nested structure — function calls, bracket matching, depth-first traversal, undo history. A queue is first-in, first-out: enqueue at the back, dequeue at the front. It models fair service and breadth-first traversal, such as exploring a road network by distance from the start. - A plain array queue wastes space as the front advances; a circular buffer reuses it. - A deque allows both ends in constant time. Hash tables A hash table maps a key to a bucket by computing h(key), aiming for constant-time average lookup, insertion and deletion. Collisions are unavoidable; separate chaining stores a list per bucket, while open addressing probes other slots in a fixed sequence. - Performance depends on the load factor, the ratio of stored keys to buckets. - Small tables and poor hash functions turn expected O(1) into O(n). - Never rely on iteration order, and rehash by doubling when the load factor passes a threshold. Load factor α = n / m Trees and heaps A binary search tree keeps smaller keys left and larger keys right, so search costs the height of the tree: O(log n) when balanced, O(n) when degenerate. Balanced trees rebalance on insertion and guarantee logarithmic height. - A heap keeps only a partial order — every parent smaller than its children for a min-heap — which is enough for a priority queue. - Push and pop cost O(log n), reading the extreme costs O(1), and the structure lives in a flat array. Balance and rotations A search tree is only logarithmic while it stays balanced. An AVL tree keeps, at every node, the heights of the two subtrees within one of each other; when an insertion breaks that rule, a rotation restores it. - A single rotation fixes an outside-heavy shape, while a double rotation fixes the zig-zag inside shape. - Rotations are local pointer surgery: constant time, but they must update parent links and the stored heights. - Red–black trees relax the rule to a colouring scheme that needs at most a constant number of rotations per insertion. - In exams, name the invariant first, apply the rotation second, and update the metadata third. subjects.subtitle: How transport systems are operated, scheduled and priced
subjects.summary: Networks are built once but operated every day. This page covers how services are scheduled, how capacity and reliability are measured, and how pricing and demand management shape who travels when.
subjects.text: Networks are built once but operated every day. This page covers how services are scheduled, how capacity and reliability are measured, and how pricing and demand management shape who travels when. Operations is supply meeting demand A transport system is a physical network operated to a timetable. Supply is what the operator can deliver: vehicles, drivers, track and platform space. Demand is when and where people want to travel, and it is rarely smooth. Operations is the daily reconciliation of the two. Three decisions dominate: - Service plan — sets routes, stops and frequencies. - Schedule — turns the plan into vehicle and crew duties. - Control — adjusts the plan in real time when traffic, weather or incidents break it. Good operations are judged by what passengers experience — wait, crowding, reliability — not only by what the timetable promises. Headway is the master variable Frequency and headway are two views of the same fact. A service with headway h seconds runs 3600/h vehicles per hour. If a bus every 400 s carries a practical capacity of 102 passengers, the line offers about 918 spaces per hour per direction; demand above that cannot be carried without more vehicles, bigger vehicles or demand management. Headway also sets the passenger cost. With arrivals spread at random, the expected wait is half a headway, so cutting a 12-minute headway to 6 minutes removes three minutes from the average trip. Frequency and headway f = 3600 / h Line capacity C = f · c Mean wait, random arrivals E[w] = h / 2 Fleet size follows from round trip time The number of vehicles needed is the round trip time divided by the headway, rounded up. A route that takes 60 minutes to return needs nine vehicles in service to hold a 400 s headway. This is why a small delay on a long route is expensive: layover and recovery time have to sit inside the round trip, or the timetable cannot be kept. Crews need the same arithmetic. Driver duties must respect legal limits on continuous driving and rest, so schedules are built from duty blocks rather than vehicle movements alone. Fleet size at constant headway N = ⌈Tround / h⌉ Signals, stages and the cycle A signal junction trades movements in time rather than space. Conflicting streams run in separate stages; a stage plan lists which movements get green together, and the cycle time is the interval before the pattern repeats. The green split divides the cycle among the stages, less the lost time spent starting and clearing each one. Capacity at a stop line is set by saturation flow — the maximum vehicles per hour a lane can discharge during green — multiplied by the proportion of the cycle that is green. A lane short of capacity queues into the next cycle, so the split, not just the total green, decides delay. The observed cycle rarely equals the sum of the greens: measure it at the site. Lane capacity at signals Q = s × (g / c) Saturation flow s = 3600 / hs Dwell time and stop operations At a stop, the door cycle governs the busiest part of the journey. Dwell time is the interval from doors open to doors closed: alighting and boarding passengers move in parallel where possible, so the longer of the two flows plus the door opening and closing time sets the dwell. Dwell matters because it multiplies with passengers: each additional boarding passenger costs roughly a fixed time, and at busy stops dwell dominates the stop's capacity. Fare media make the difference — smart cards and open boarding are faster than cash and on-bus ticket sales, so the boarding rate is a design variable, not a constant. Dwell time D = max(talight, tboard) + tdoors Crew and vehicle scheduling Vehicles and drivers are scheduled separately. Vehicle blocks run from depot to depot; crew duties run from sign-on to sign-off and must respect legal limits on continuous driving, breaks and spread-over time, so a duty rarely equals a vehicle block. subjects.subtitle: Flow in channels, pipe networks and the rainfall-runoff process
subjects.summary: Water on its way to the sea: uniform and varied flow in open channels, Manning's equation, specific energy and hydraulic jumps, then pipe losses, the rainfall-runoff chain, the rational method and return periods.
subjects.text: Water on its way to the sea: uniform and varied flow in open channels, Manning's equation, specific energy and hydraulic jumps, then pipe losses, the rainfall-runoff chain, the rational method and return periods. Two ways water flows Open-channel flow has a free surface at atmospheric pressure; gravity drives it, and the depth can rise and fall. Pipe flow runs full, driven by a pressure gradient, with a fixed cross-section. Open-channel depth is set by the bed slope and the downstream control; a full pipe's head loss follows from discharge and roughness. Flow is uniform when depth, area and velocity do not change along the reach — an equilibrium between gravity and friction. Gradually varied flow changes slowly, as behind a weir; rapidly varied flow changes over a few depths, as at a jump. Manning's equation Manning's equation estimates mean velocity from the channel geometry, the bed slope and a roughness coefficient. It uses the hydraulic radius R = A/P — area divided by wetted perimeter — because friction acts along the perimeter. It is not a derivation but a fit to measurements. The roughness coefficient n is empirical and absorbs vegetation and bed irregularities. Values are indicative: smooth concrete around 0.012–0.015, earth channels 0.020–0.030, vegetated streams higher. The 1/n form applies to SI units only. Manning velocity V = (1/n) R^(2/3) S^(1/2) Specific energy and critical depth Specific energy is the head of the water relative to the channel bed: E = y + V²/(2g). At a fixed discharge per unit width q, the E–y curve is a parabola with a minimum, and for any energy above it there are two possible depths — the alternate depths. The minimum is the critical depth, at Fr = 1. Flow is subcritical when Fr < 1 (controlled from downstream) and supercritical when Fr 1 (controlled from upstream). A control such as a weir forces the depth to critical and fixes the upstream profile. Specific energy E = y + V²/(2g) Critical depth, rectangular channel yc = (q²/g)^(1/3) Froude number Fr = V / √(g D) The hydraulic jump When supercritical flow meets an obstruction or a rise in tailwater, it jumps to subcritical flow across a short turbulent transition. Depth rises, velocity falls, and much of the kinetic energy is dissipated as heat — which is why jumps are built below spillways to protect the bed downstream. The depth change is found from momentum, since the energy loss is not known in advance. For a rectangular channel the conjugate depths follow a relation in the approaching Froude number, and the loss grows steeply with jump strength. An oscillating jump is unstable and should be designed out. Conjugate depths y₂/y₁ = ½ ( √(1 + 8 Fr₁²) − 1 ) Pipe networks and friction In a full pipe the head loss has two parts: friction, proportional to length and velocity squared, and minor losses at bends, valves and fittings, quoted through a coefficient K. The Darcy–Weisbach equation is the standard form; f comes from the Moody chart and depends on Reynolds number and relative roughness ε/D. Networks add continuity at every junction and a single head at each node. Parallel pipes share the same head loss, so flow splits in inverse proportion to resistance; pipes in series share the same discharge and add their losses. Large networks are solved iteratively by adjusting flows until the heads close. Darcy–Weisbach head loss hf = f (L/D) V²/(2g) Well hydraulics in an unconfined aquifer Pumping a well in an unconfined aquifer creates a cone of depression: radial flow converges on the well, and Darcy's law integrated over the cone gives the discharge in terms of the water levels in two observation wells at distances r₁ and r₂: Q = π k (h₂² − h₁²) / ln(r₂/r₁), with k the permeability and h the saturated thickness at each well. A pumping test therefore measures k in the ground at full scale, rather than in a small sample: pump at constant discharge until the levels stabilise, read h₁ and h₂, and solve for k. subjects.subtitle: Reinforced concrete members to Hong Kong practice
subjects.summary: Reinforced concrete design turns a required strength into steel areas, bar sizes and cover. It links limit-state loading to bending, shear, slab and column checks, then closes with detailing and serviceability.
subjects.text: Reinforced concrete design turns a required strength into steel areas, bar sizes and cover. It links limit-state loading to bending, shear, slab and column checks, then closes with detailing and serviceability. Limit state design in concrete Concrete resists compression well and tension poorly, so reinforcement is placed where a member would otherwise crack. Limit state design replaces one global safety factor with partial factors applied separately to loads and materials. - At the ultimate limit state (ULS) the member must not collapse. - At the serviceability limit state (SLS) deflection and cracking must stay acceptable in normal use. - The characteristic concrete strength fcu is the 28-day cube strength; fy is the characteristic yield strength of the reinforcement. Never mix the two states. A section can pass ULS and still sag or crack unacceptably, and an SLS check says nothing about collapse. Design load wu = 1.4 Gk + 1.6 Qk Bending of a singly reinforced section A rectangular section in bending is designed from a stress block in the concrete and a tensile force in the steel. The K value measures how heavily the concrete is stressed: K = M / (fcu b d²) where b is the section width and d the effective depth, measured from the compression face to the centroid of the tension steel. - Below the limiting K′ = 0.156, a section can be singly reinforced. - The lever arm is z = d [0.5 + √(0.25 − K/0.9)], capped at 0.95d. - The steel area follows from As = M / (0.87 fy z). K value K = M / (fcu b d²) Lever arm z = d [0.5 + √(0.25 − K/0.9)] ≤ 0.95 d Required tension steel As = M / (0.87 fy z) Moment coefficients for continuous beams For a continuous beam under uniform loading, a full elastic analysis can be replaced by tabulated moment coefficients when three conditions hold: - the spans differ by no more than about 15% of the longest, - the loading is essentially uniform, - the live load does not exceed the dead load. The design moment is then M = β F L, where F = w L is the total design load on the span and β is the coefficient for the position. Typical values are 0.04F at an outer support, 0.075F near midspan of an end span, 0.086F at the first interior support, and 0.063F at midspan of interior spans and at interior supports. The first interior support moment is the largest, which is why top steel is heaviest there; the associated shear forces follow from the same table or from the free body of each span. The coefficients assume monolithic construction and fairly uniform stiffness along the beam. Heavily haunched or irregular frames need an elastic analysis instead. Design moment from coefficients M = β F L Position Coefficient β on F = w L Flanged beams and compression steel Beams cast with a slab act as T- or L-sections, because a width of slab joins the compression zone. The effective flange width is limited to a fraction of the span and of the beam spacing, so only slab close to the web is counted. Check where the stress block sits: its depth is s = 2(d − z). If s does not exceed the flange thickness hf, the section behaves as a rectangle of the full flange width and the usual K and z expressions apply. If the block reaches into the web, design as a true T-section. When K exceeds K′, deepen the beam or add compression steel, sized from the excess moment and the depth between the steel layers. Effective flange width and the T-beam sequence A T-beam counts only part of the slab as its flange. The overhang on each side of the web is limited to about 0.2 times the clear distance to the adjacent beam plus 0.1 times the effective span, and for an edge (L) beam the span term is reduced to about 85% of that value. Worked from a beam grid with 4 m spacing and 5 m spans, the effective flange width came to 680 mm, giving 930 mm in total once the 250 mm web was added — far less than the full spacing. subjects.subtitle: Road design, traffic flow, pavements and safety
subjects.summary: Roads are designed as a hierarchy of routes where geometry, pavement and traffic behaviour must agree with the speed expected. This page links alignment, sight distance, pavement and traffic flow into one design story.
subjects.text: Roads are designed as a hierarchy of routes where geometry, pavement and traffic behaviour must agree with the speed expected. This page links alignment, sight distance, pavement and traffic flow into one design story. Road hierarchy and design control A road network is organised by function: - Primary or trunk roads carry long-distance traffic at high speed with limited access. - Secondary roads link districts. - Distributors spread traffic into neighbourhoods. - Local roads give frontage access at low speed. The key trade-off is between mobility and access. Every driveway or side road joining a fast route adds a conflict point, so access is deliberately restricted on higher classes. Signs, markings and junctions should tell a driver what class of road they are on, so speed and behaviour match expectations. Mixing functions on one road is where most safety and capacity problems begin. Design speed and geometric consistency Design speed is the speed chosen as the basis of geometric design: it fixes minimum radius, superelevation, sight distance and crest curve length. The road must be credible at that speed, because drivers read the geometry and settle on a speed that feels comfortable. Geometric consistency matters more than any single element. A long straight followed by a tight bend invites too much speed into the curve, so elements should change gradually. The cross-section follows the same logic: carriageway width, emergency shoulders, verges for pedestrians, kerbs and the camber or crossfall that drains the surface. Stopping and overtaking sight distance Stopping sight distance (SSD) is the distance a driver needs to stop before an unexpected object at the design speed. It is the reaction distance plus the braking distance: SSD = 0.278 V t + V² / [254 (f + G)] with V in km/h, reaction time t in seconds, longitudinal friction f and gradient G as a decimal. Uphill gradients shorten braking and downhill gradients lengthen it, so the check uses the steepest downgrade. Overtaking sight distance is longer again, because the manoeuvre must see far enough to pass and return safely. Where it cannot be provided, the road should offer safe passing places or be marked no-overtaking. Stopping sight distance SSD = 0.278 V t + V² / [254 (f + G)] Horizontal alignment and superelevation Horizontal alignment is a sequence of straights, circular curves and transition curves. For a circular curve of radius R, the superelevation e and the side friction f together balance the centrifugal force: e + f = V² / (127 R) with V in km/h and R in metres. Required superelevation therefore rises with the square of speed and falls as the radius increases. A transition curve eases the change in curvature, lets the superelevation be applied gradually and gives the driver time to steer. Tight curves are also widened slightly, because the rear wheels of a long vehicle track inside the front wheels. Superelevation balance e + f = V² / (127 R) Vertical alignment: gradients and curves Vertical alignment uses gradients and parabolic curves. Maximum gradients are limited because long upgrades slow heavy vehicles and steep downgrades overload brakes. On a crest, the curve must keep the road surface below the driver's line of sight. When the sight distance S is shorter than the curve length L, L = A S² / 647, where A is the algebraic change in gradient in percent. If the sight distance is longer than the curve, L = 2S − 647/A. Sag curves are governed by comfort and headlight sight distance, using a criterion such as L = A V² / 395. The ratio K = L/A should exceed the minimum for the design speed. subjects.subtitle: Foundations, retaining structures, slopes and ground improvement
subjects.summary: Geotechnical design turns ground investigation into foundations, retaining structures and slopes that are safe against failure and acceptable in settlement. Almost every decision depends on effective stress, drainage and the water table.
subjects.text: Geotechnical design turns ground investigation into foundations, retaining structures and slopes that are safe against failure and acceptable in settlement. Almost every decision depends on effective stress, drainage and the water table. Site investigation and the ground model Every geotechnical design starts by turning a site into a ground model: the sequence of soil and rock layers, their strength and stiffness, and the position of the water table. - Desk study of maps and records first, then boreholes and in-situ tests, then laboratory testing. - The standard penetration test and cone penetration test give a continuous feel for density and strength with depth; sampling gives parameters that tests in the ground cannot. - Pore pressure reduces effective stress and changes every strength and settlement calculation. One borehole proves one point, not a site, so parameters are selected as characteristic values and combined with partial factors. Ultimate bearing capacity Bearing capacity asks whether the ground can carry the foundation load without a shear failure. For a strip footing the ultimate pressure is qu = c′ Nc + q′ Nq + 0.5 γ B Nγ, where c′ is effective cohesion, q′ the surcharge at foundation level, γ the soil unit weight, B the footing width, and N the bearing capacity factors that grow with friction angle. - Shape factors adjust the result for square and circular footings. - A water table in the failure zone reduces the effective unit weight. - A factor of safety or a set of partial factors brings the ultimate capacity down to an allowable or design value. Terzaghi bearing capacity, strip footing qu = c′ Nc + q′ Nq + 0.5 γ B Nγ φ′ (degrees) Nc Nq Nγ Eccentric loading and contact pressure Real columns arrive with moment as well as load, so the contact pressure under a footing is rarely uniform. The eccentricity is e = M/Q. - While the resultant stays within the middle third of the base — e ≤ B/6 — the whole base remains in contact and the pressure is trapezoidal: qmax,min = Q/(B L) (1 ± 6e/B). - Once e exceeds B/6, part of the base lifts off and contact is lost over a width B − 2e from the load side; the peak pressure then concentrates near the edge: qmax = 4Q / [3 L (B − 2e)]. The design response is the effective area concept: shrink the footing to the loaded zone B′ = B − 2e, check bearing on the reduced dimensions, and accept that a wide footing with a small moment is usually better than a narrow one with a large one. Peak pressure, resultant within the middle third qmax = Q / (B L) (1 + 6e/B) Peak pressure, partial contact qmax = 4 Q / [3 L (B − 2e)] Condition Contact Pressure distribution Peak pressure Settlement and serviceability Serviceability is checked by estimating settlement. Sands settle almost immediately, mainly by elastic compression; clays settle slowly as excess pore water drains, which is consolidation. - Elastic settlement is often estimated as Se = q B (1 − ν²) I / E, where q is the applied pressure, ν Poisson's ratio, E the soil modulus and I an influence factor for shape and depth. - For a normally consolidated clay layer, the one-dimensional consolidation settlement is Sc = [Cc H / (1 + e0)] log[(σ′0 + Δσ′)/σ′0], with compression index Cc, initial void ratio e0, layer thickness H and the effective stress increase Δσ′. Total settlement matters, but differential settlement is what cracks structures, so it is checked between adjacent supports. subjects.title: BIM & 3D GIS
subjects.subtitle: Combining building information models with spatial data
subjects.summary: Building information models describe individual assets with rich data, while 3D GIS describes the ground they sit on. Combining them needs open standards, a common data environment and a shared coordinate system.
subjects.text: Building information models describe individual assets with rich data, while 3D GIS describes the ground they sit on. Combining them needs open standards, a common data environment and a shared coordinate system. BIM is an information model, not a drawing A building information model is a set of objects — walls, slabs, pipes, spaces — each carrying geometry, relationships and attributes. Because each object is defined once, the same model can produce drawings, schedules, quantities, coordination checks and handover data. A federated model combines discipline models into one coordination environment while each author keeps control of their own file. Model quality, naming and information structure matter as much as the drawing itself. The model is also the record handed to the operator at completion, so its information should be defined by the people who will use it, not only by those who build it. The dimensions of BIM Information models are described by dimensions. Three dimensions give geometry; the higher dimensions add information that other people use. - The numbering is a communication device rather than a formal standard, so agree on what each dimension means on a project. - The value of the higher dimensions depends on the lower ones. - A schedule or cost model built on badly named and uncoordinated objects produces confident answers that are wrong. Dimension Adds Typical use IFC and open exchange IFC (Industry Foundation Classes) is the open, vendor-neutral schema for exchanging building models. It defines entities such as walls, spaces and properties, and the relationships between them, so a model authored in one tool can be read in another without losing its meaning. - Exchange is controlled by model view definitions, which select the subset of the schema needed for a purpose such as coordination or quantity take-off. - Property sets carry the attributes a receiving party needs, and classification systems align objects with work breakdowns. - IFC does not replace native formats; it is the contract between them. CityGML and semantic city models CityGML is the open standard for 3D city models: thematic classes such as buildings, terrain, roads and vegetation, organised by graded levels of detail from a block model up to full interiors. Unlike IFC, which describes one building's components for design and construction, CityGML describes many assets and their context for analysis and administration. Objects carry semantics as well as surfaces, so a query can ask for all residential floors above a flood level rather than a bare mesh. Because the two schemas overlap but do not align one-to-one, converting between them needs a defined mapping, and every conversion loses some information on the way. Aspect IFC CityGML The common data environment A common data environment (CDE) is the single agreed source of project information. Models and documents are held in containers and move through controlled states: work in progress, shared, published and archived. Only shared or published information may be relied on by other parties. - Information requirements — what information, in what format, at what date — are defined before work starts, and the delivery plan says who provides it. - Version control, naming and status codes show which file is current, which solves the oldest problem in coordination. - Where several organisations contribute, the environment also records who approved each container and when, so responsibility stays traceable. GIS data models and 3D city models GIS describes the world with spatial data models. Vector models store points, lines and polygons with attributes and topology, suited to networks and boundaries; raster models store grid cells, suited to continuous surfaces such as terrain and imagery; TINs represent terrain as triangulated surfaces. subjects.title: Service Learning
subjects.subtitle: Engineering in the community: listening, designing and reflecting
subjects.summary: Working with a community partner on a real project while learning from the work itself. It covers needs assessment, co-design, delivery, honest evaluation and structured reflection, with an emphasis on reciprocity rather than charity.
subjects.text: Working with a community partner on a real project while learning from the work itself. It covers needs assessment, co-design, delivery, honest evaluation and structured reflection, with an emphasis on reciprocity rather than charity. More than volunteering Service learning is a course with a partner. Students work on a real community project, usually with a school, charity or residents' group, and the experience carries academic credit because it is assessed through reflection and evidence of learning. The difference from volunteering is reciprocity: the community gains something it asked for, and the students gain knowledge they could not get from a lecture. Charity does something for people; service learning does something with them. Start with a needs assessment Never design before listening. A needs assessment asks who is affected, what they already have, and what they say is missing. - Interview the people who will use the output, not only the staff who host you. - Walk the site rather than reading about it. - Take an asset-based view: a school may lack equipment but has a hall, a timetable and teachers who know their students. - Record what the partner asked for, so the brief is theirs as well as yours. Co-design, not delivery from above Participatory design gives users real decisions, not a consultation at the end. - Prototype early and cheaply — a paper model, a draft lesson, a walk-through — because people react to something concrete far better than to an abstract proposal. - Watch for barriers of language, reading level, mobility, cost and timing. - Agree what is fixed and what is open before a workshop starts, so the group knows where its power actually lies. Deliver within real constraints A service project is still a project: scope, schedule, budget and risk. Partners have calendars, rules and busy staff, and a plan that ignores a school's examination period will fail. - Plan for safeguarding and consent when working with children or vulnerable adults. - Check insurance and site safety before the first session. - Build capacity so the work survives your departure: leave instructions, materials and a named contact. Reflection is the learning Reflection is not a diary of what happened; it is structured thinking that connects the experience to theory and to your own practice. The Gibbs cycle gives one route: describe the situation, name your feelings, evaluate what went well, analyse why, conclude what you would do differently, and commit to an action. Strong reflection is specific, admits difficulty and shows changed understanding. Incidents are evidence; general claims are not. Gibbs reflective cycle Description → Feelings → Evaluation → Analysis → Conclusion → Action plan Evaluate impact honestly Outputs are countable — a workshop ran, a model was built. Outcomes are changes in knowledge, behaviour or confidence; impact is the longer-term difference. - Ask the partner how they will judge success. - Use a short before-and-after measure rather than impression alone. - Report what did not work, who was left out and what you would change. Honest evaluation serves a partner better than a polished success story. Impact chain Output → Outcome → Impact Partner-led success criterion Success = what the partner said they needed, evidenced Aspect Volunteering Service learning Quick reflection frames Gibbs is not the only route. The What? So what? Now what? frame compresses reflection to three moves: describe the incident, explain why it matters and what it teaches, then commit to a change. It suits short reflections and quick debriefs after a session. Whatever the model, the evidence test is the same: a good reflection names one incident, connects it to a concept, and ends with a changed intention. "The students were quiet" is a diary; "the students were quiet until we switched to hands-on building, which showed me that engagement follows activity, so next time I will plan less talk" is reflection. subjects.subtitle: Search, learning and generative models in engineering
subjects.summary: Artificial intelligence is the engineering of systems that perceive, reason and learn. This page covers search, knowledge representation, learning, neural networks, generative models and how to evaluate them honestly.
subjects.text: Artificial intelligence is the engineering of systems that perceive, reason and learn. This page covers search, knowledge representation, learning, neural networks, generative models and how to evaluate them honestly. What AI asks of an engineer AI is not one algorithm but a family of methods for acting under uncertainty. The classical framing separates perception, reasoning, learning and action, and asks what the system must decide, what it can observe and what being wrong would cost. Most deployed AI is narrow: excellent at one task and unable to transfer. That is the design scope rather than a fault, and writing it down is the first engineering decision. Search: from a goal to a path Many problems are posed as a state space: states, actions, a start, a goal and a cost per step. - Breadth-first search finds the fewest steps. - Depth-first saves memory but can wander. - Uniform-cost search expands the cheapest prefix first. - A\ adds a heuristic estimate of the remaining cost. If the heuristic never overestimates — if it is admissible — A returns a least-cost path without exploring everything. The heuristic is the whole design: too weak is nearly blind, too optimistic loses optimality. A evaluation function f(n) = g(n) + h(n) Knowledge representation A reasoning system needs a model of the world it can manipulate. - Logic represents facts and rules and derives conclusions mechanically. - Frames and semantic networks group attributes around objects. - Ontologies and knowledge graphs fix a shared vocabulary so different systems mean the same thing by the same term. Engineering knowledge is messy and uncertain. Probabilistic models, rules carrying confidence and explicit assumptions record what is not known, which matters as much as what is. Machine learning: learning a mapping A supervised model learns a mapping from features to labels using examples. Data are split into training, validation and test sets; the test set is touched once, at the end, to estimate generalisation. A model that fits its training data but fails on new data is overfitting. The remedy is discipline, not complexity: representative data, regularisation, simpler models and a validation loop that does not quietly tune the test score. Always report a naive baseline. Neural networks and deep learning A single artificial neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias and passes the result through a non-linear activation function. Stacking layers represents complicated relationships. Training adjusts the weights to reduce a loss, typically by gradient descent with backpropagation supplying the gradient for every weight. Depth helps because early layers learn general features and later layers combine them. It also makes optimisation harder, data demand greater and behaviour less interpretable. Artificial neuron a = φ(Σ wᵢ xᵢ + b) Gradient descent update w ← w − η ∂L/∂w Generative models A generative model learns the distribution of its training data and produces new samples. - Large language models predict the next token from the preceding ones, so generation is repeated prediction. - Diffusion models add noise to data in training and learn to reverse that process when sampling. Generation is sampling, not recall. That explains the fluency and the hallucination: a plausible continuation is not a true one. Autoregressive generation p(x₁, …, xT) = Π p(xt | x<t) Evaluation is part of the design A model is only as good as the evidence used to judge it. Split data honestly, keep a hold-out set, and choose metrics that match the cost of error. In defect detection, precision asks how many flagged defects were real, while recall asks how many real defects were caught; a high-accuracy model that always says no defect is useless. Evaluation also covers latency, robustness to shifted inputs, calibration and test-data leakage. Generative output needs rubric-based human assessment, with criteria fixed in advance. subjects.subtitle: Junctions, rail and the infrastructure behind movement
subjects.summary: Junctions and rail lines are sized by the capacity they must deliver, not by the space they occupy. This page covers priority junctions, roundabouts, signal capacity, railway headways and the standards that hold them together.
subjects.text: Junctions and rail lines are sized by the capacity they must deliver, not by the space they occupy. This page covers priority junctions, roundabouts, signal capacity, railway headways and the standards that hold them together. Design is a capacity question A transport facility is designed for a design-year demand expressed in passenger car units per hour rather than raw vehicles, because a heavy lorry occupies more road space than a car. The key ratio is the degree of saturation, demand divided by capacity; the key outputs are delay and queue length. Capacity alone does not choose a junction type. Safety, land, pedestrians, cost and the surrounding network all constrain the answer, which is why standards offer layouts rather than one solution. Type Capacity driver Strength Weakness Priority junctions: gap acceptance At a give-way junction the minor arm must find a gap in the major flow. Its capacity therefore falls as the conflicting flow rises, and the shape of that fall follows gap acceptance theory: a driver needs a critical gap before emerging, and successive vehicles follow at the follow-up time. The practical conclusion is that the minor approach is the bottleneck, and its capacity is sensitive to major-road volume, visibility and turning proportions. An extra minor lane or a flare helps only when lanes, not gaps, are the constraint. Minor-arm capacity (gap acceptance) C = q e^(−q tc / 3600) / [1 − e^(−q tf / 3600)] Roundabouts: circulating flow sets entry capacity A roundabout entry gives way to the circulating flow, so entry capacity is a function of the traffic already on the ring. Empirical models of the linear form below are fitted to observed behaviour; the coefficients depend on the entry geometry rather than being universal constants. Geometry matters because it controls speed and gap acceptance. Entry deflection, entry width, flare length and island radius all change how quickly vehicles can enter. A mini-roundabout simplifies the crossing points, but because its island is traversable and lanes are shared it can become overloaded quickly. Roundabout entry capacity Centry = a − b qc Signals: saturation flow and green ratio A signal approach discharges at its saturation flow while the green is fully used — roughly 1,800 to 2,000 pcu/h per lane under ideal conditions. Over a cycle of length C with effective green g, capacity is saturation flow times the green ratio. The flow ratio y = q/s measures how much saturation flow the demand needs, and the degree of saturation X = q/c compares demand with capacity. Lost time — start-up and clearance in every stage — is why a short cycle wastes a larger share of green, and why Webster's formula trades that waste against the delay of a long cycle. The field method counts departing vehicles during saturated cycles — green periods that end with a queue still present — and needs at least about five queued vehicles to be reliable. The first few vehicles are excluded because they are still overcoming start-up lost time, so only the steady headway portion counts: s = 3600 n / tg, where n is the number of vehicles counted over the saturated portion of green of length tg. - Gradient, turning radius, lane width and the vehicle mix each justify a correction factor. - The measurement must average enough cycles on a representative lane of the approach — a straight-ahead or mixed lane, not an exclusive turning lane — because one congested minute is not a saturation flow. - Where the junction justifies it, direct measurement beats the empirical adjustment equations, which is why the manual prescribes it for detailed signal plans. subjects.subtitle: Law, ethics, contracts and the engineer's public role
subjects.summary: Engineering decisions carry legal and ethical weight. This page covers the Hong Kong legal framework, contract basics, negligence, professional ethics and the statutory duties that protect safety and the environment.
subjects.text: Engineering decisions carry legal and ethical weight. This page covers the Hong Kong legal framework, contract basics, negligence, professional ethics and the statutory duties that protect safety and the environment. Common law in a statute-based city Hong Kong's legal system continues the common law tradition: courts decide cases and earlier decisions bind later ones through precedent. Statutes — ordinances and their subsidiary regulations — sit alongside the common law and can override it where they conflict. The difference between civil and criminal proceedings matters to an engineer: - Civil disputes are decided on the balance of probabilities. - Criminal charges must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. - A construction dispute is usually civil even when the conduct involved was careless. Burden of proof civil: balance of probabilities · criminal: beyond reasonable doubt Contract: offer, acceptance, consideration A contract is a voluntary agreement the law will enforce. Formation needs offer and acceptance, consideration in the sense of something of value each side gives, intention to create legal relations, capacity and legality. - A reply that changes the terms is a counter-offer, which kills the original offer; silence is not acceptance. - Simple contracts may be oral, written or made by conduct. - A deed must be signed, sealed and delivered and needs no consideration. - Formalities matter because they change remedies and the limitation period — broadly six years for a simple contract and twelve years for a specialty. Formation test offer + acceptance + consideration + intention + capacity + legality Misrepresentation and the remedies for breach Not every false statement is a breach. A misrepresentation is a pre-contractual statement of fact that is untrue and induces the contract. The remedy follows the wrong: - Fraudulent if made knowingly or recklessly. - Negligent if made carelessly without reasonable grounds. - Innocent if honestly believed on reasonable grounds. Expectation damages put the claimant where performance would have left them — lost profit and consequential loss — while reliance damages repay wasted expenditure. Where money is not enough, specific performance or an injunction may be ordered, and a quantum meruit claim recovers reasonable remuneration for work accepted without an agreed price. Misrepresentation categories fraudulent (knowing) → negligent (careless) → innocent (honest) Type Maker's state of mind Typical remedy Breach, damages and risk allocation When a party fails to perform, the innocent party claims damages. The usual aim is to put the claimant in the position as if the contract had been performed, subject to the duty to mitigate loss. Construction contracts allocate risk explicitly through variations, extension-of-time clauses and exclusion clauses. Delay is handled by liquidated damages, a pre-agreed sum per week of delay. - Such a clause is enforceable only if it is a genuine pre-estimate of loss. - A figure designed to frighten the other side is an unenforceable penalty. - Standard forms of contract exist because that balance has been tested in practice. Liquidated damages LD = r × w, capped at c × contract sum Negligence and the duty of care Tort addresses harm done outside contract. Negligence requires a duty of care, a breach of the standard expected of a reasonable engineer, and loss caused by that breach. - Causation is tested by asking whether the loss would have happened but for the breach, and a wrongdoer generally takes the victim as found. - Defences include contributory negligence, which reduces damages, and voluntary acceptance of risk. - Employers are vicariously liable for employees acting in the course of employment. - Safety failures can attract criminal liability as well as civil claims. subjects.title: Discovering Chinese History in Hong Kong
subjects.subtitle: Hong Kong's past through places, people and sources
subjects.summary: Hong Kong's past before and beyond the colonial story: migration and lineage society, the fishing and salt economy, quarry labour, wartime rupture and post-war industry. It is also a lesson in how historians read inscriptions, genealogies and landscapes.
subjects.text: Hong Kong's past before and beyond the colonial story: migration and lineage society, the fishing and salt economy, quarry labour, wartime rupture and post-war industry. It is also a lesson in how historians read inscriptions, genealogies and landscapes. Read the place, not just the treaty Hong Kong's history is often dated from 1842, but that is a colonial frame. For centuries the area belonged to the administrative and cultural world of the Pearl River Delta, passing through counties such as 番禺 Panyu, 東莞 Dongguan and finally 新安 Xin'an. Reading the past from the Chinese side means starting with migration, lineage society, coastal trade and the sea, then treating the colonial period as one chapter in a longer story. Source criticism Provenance → Purpose → Perspective → Corroboration Migration and the great clans Most settled communities in the New Territories trace ancestry back to migration during the Song and Yuan periods. Five lineages dominate the written record — the 鄧 Tang, 侯 Hau, 廖 Liu, 文 Man and 彭 Pang, usually called the 新界五大族. A lineage was more than a family: - ancestral halls - 族譜 genealogies - communal land held in trusts - 圍村 walled villages These let a clan organise labour, defend resources and assert status. Genealogies are useful and partial: they record what a lineage wished remembered. Reasoning chain Claim → Evidence → Context → Qualification Fishing, salt and a maritime economy Before industry, the sea paid the bills. Salt evaporation fields on the western shore, notably around 大澳 Tai O, produced revenue for the imperial state, while fishing communities — including boat-dwelling groups known as 蛋家 Tanka — worked coastal waters and markets. 屯門 Tuen Mun was already a recognised anchorage and trading stop in the Tang period, where foreign ships waited for the monsoon. 天后 Tin Hau temples mark this world; their inscriptions often list the donors and land given to maintain them. Granite, quarries and stonecutters Granite underlies much of the territory, and quarrying grew into an export trade. 石匠 stonecutters worked sites from 鯉魚門 Lei Yue Mun to 鑽石山 Diamond Hill, cutting blocks for local building and for ports further afield. Because stone is heavy, the trade shaped roads, piers and settlement around the quarries. Quarry history links geology, labour and shipping, and it shows that the landscape itself can be a historical source. Colonial development, occupation and industry The colonial period reshaped the coast quickly: - the cession of Hong Kong Island in 1841–42 - the addition of Kowloon - the 1898 lease of the New Territories These brought surveys, roads, railways, reservoirs and a new legal order. The Japanese occupation of 1941–45 broke that system and left the population reduced and hungry. After 1945 the economy moved from entrepôt trade to manufacturing and then services, with public housing, new towns and container ports following. Reading the evidence History is argued from evidence, and Hong Kong has many kinds: archaeological finds, temple and 碑銘 stone inscriptions, genealogies, land deeds, colonial maps and archives, newspapers and oral testimony. Each answers some questions and is silent on others — an inscription may list donors but not the worshippers who could not read. Interpretation adds another layer, because a restored building is also a choice about which past to present. Separate what a source says from what the historian infers. The Lei Cheng Uk tomb (李鄭屋漢墓), an Eastern Han brick tomb uncovered in the 1950s, carries bricks stamped 大吉番禺 — "great fortune, Panyu" — evidence that the area was administered within Panyu county some 1,800 years before the colonial treaty. It is a reminder that the region's written history has a deep, buried prelude.
