subjects.subtitle: Sensors, embedded intelligence and connected infrastructure
subjects.summary: Sensors, small computers, networks and models working together under real constraints. The subject is less about the cleverest algorithm than about latency, energy, bandwidth and freshness, and what those trade-offs mean for connected infrastructure.
subjects.text: Sensors, small computers, networks and models working together under real constraints. The subject is less about the cleverest algorithm than about latency, energy, bandwidth and freshness, and what those trade-offs mean for connected infrastructure. The loop, not the device AIoT puts inference close to where data is made. A system senses with transducers, conditions the signal on a microcontroller, moves it over a network, and acts on a decision. What separates it from ordinary IoT is that a model makes the decision, often on the device itself. The design question is never accuracy alone: it is accuracy per unit of energy, latency and bandwidth. A bridge strain sensor reporting in milliseconds solves a different problem from a soil probe that wakes once an hour. Nyquist sampling rule fs 2 fmax Sensing, sampling and the microcontroller A sensor converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal, and an ADC turns that into numbers at a fixed sampling rate. Real readings carry noise and drift, so calibrate against a reference and filter, remembering that every filter adds delay. A microcontroller provides GPIO pins, timers and buses such as I²C and SPI for local chips, and it must be duty-cycled: radio and sensing dominate the power budget, so sleeping between samples is what makes a battery last for years. ADC resolution ΔV = Vref / 2^n Networking choices No single radio fits every deployment. Above the link layer, MQTT is the usual messaging pattern: devices publish to a broker on a topic such as site/42/temperature, and subscribers receive it. QoS levels 0, 1 and 2 trade duplicates against delivery guarantees, and a retained message stops a late subscriber from seeing stale state. Publishing a reading with MQTT client.publish('site/42/strain', payload, qos=1) client.subscribe('site/42/command') Radio Typical range Data rate Power Typical use Protocols beyond MQTT MQTT is not the only way to move bytes. CoAP shrinks HTTP's request–response model onto UDP for constrained nodes, with confirmable messages and an observe mode for server push; it suits a battery sensor behind a gateway rather than a chatty web app. Plain HTTP/REST is easy to debug and integrate but verbose per message; WebSockets keep a persistent channel for live dashboards; AMQP adds enterprise routing for fleets of gateways. Choose by constraint, not habit: payload and header overhead, connection state, delivery guarantee, and whether the network is IP end-to-end or needs a gateway translation. A protocol that assumes always-on TCP is a poor fit for a node that wakes once an hour. Protocol Transport Pattern Best fit Edge or cloud Inference can run on the device, at a gateway, or in the cloud. Pushing it closer cuts latency and bandwidth but limits model size and energy. End-to-end latency is the sum of the stages, and the slowest stage dominates. Model compression makes edge inference practical: quantisation stores weights in 8 bits instead of 32, pruning removes small weights, and both cost a little accuracy. Treat the choice as a trade curve rather than a slogan. End-to-end latency L = tsense + tqueue + tcompute + tnetwork Service capacity C = 1 / tservice Learned controllers: from rules to gradients On-device AI is often a learned controller rather than a vision model. A rule-based layer switches on fixed thresholds; a learned layer computes a linear score from features and turns it into a probability with the sigmoid function. Training finds the weights by descending the gradient of the cross-entropy loss, which punishes confident mistakes far more than hesitant ones. The workflow matters as much as the maths: collect labelled behaviour from a working controller, extract the same features at run time, train offline, then run the small model online. Because the model learns a decision pattern rather than the physics, it reproduces the teacher's behaviour without understanding the room — which is exactly why the training data must cover the edge cases. subjects.text: How movement is measured and then predicted. It covers classified counts and origin–destination surveys, sampling and expansion, the four-step demand model, network assignment and the land-use feedback that decides whether a forecast is realistic. Planning is a chain of evidence Transport planning predicts how many people will move, where, by which mode and along which links, so that infrastructure and services can be sized before demand arrives. The classic four-step model runs: trip generation, trip distribution, mode choice and assignment. Each step needs data of a different kind, and an error at the start is not repaired by a clever model at the end. Strategic plans look decades ahead, tactical plans a few years, and operational plans a season. Counting and interviewing The basic tool is the classified count, which records volume by vehicle type and direction over a period. Counts can be manual, temporary automatic (tubes, loops, radar) or permanent; short counts are expanded to a typical day using factors. Origin–destination surveys ask where trips start and end: roadside interviews, number-plate matching, GPS traces or mobile network data. Speed surveys measure spot speed or journey time, and parking surveys record accumulation and duration. Method Measures Strength Limitation Sampling, expansion and error No survey counts everything. A sample is expanded to the population, so the expansion factor carries its sampling error with it. Sampling error falls with the square root of sample size, so quadrupling the sample halves it. Coverage bias is worse than random error — counting only weekday peaks, or only drivers who stop for an interview, measures a selected group. Neutral months and neutral days matter, and public holidays are excluded. Sample size for a proportion n = z² p (1 − p) / e² Trip generation and the O–D matrix Trip generation estimates how many trips a household or development produces, from survey data by household size, income and car ownership, or from regression. The output is a trip matrix: rows are origins, columns are destinations, and the diagonal holds intrazonal trips. Matrices are expanded from the sample to the population and balanced so row and column totals agree with control totals. Poor zoning — too coarse, or in the wrong place — distorts everything downstream. Trip generation models Trip generation is estimated either by category analysis — average trip rates per household or person in each size or income class — or by regression, which fits trips against household characteristics. A typical model regresses daily trips on household size and car ownership, giving a constant plus a rate per explanatory variable. The coefficients are not facts; they are fitted to one survey and inherit its bias. A small, unrepresentative sample produces rates that look precise and are systematically wrong. Compare fitted rates against a large citywide travel survey before using them, and keep the units — trips per household per day — attached to every coefficient. Linear trip generation model T = a + b₁ X₁ + b₂ X₂ + … Category trip rate r = T / H Distribution and mode choice Trip distribution decides where generated trips go. The gravity model allocates trips to destinations in proportion to their attractiveness and inversely to the cost of reaching them, with a deterrence function calibrated against observed travel. Mode choice then divides each flow among car, public transport and walking using generalised cost — time, fare, waiting, comfort and reliability combined. A logit model turns the utility of each option into a probability, so a small cost change produces a gradual shift rather than an all-or-nothing switch. subjects.text: Keeping built assets useful over decades: registers, condition assessment, deterioration, maintenance strategy, risk, whole-life cost and the digital tools that hold the data together. It is engineering economics applied to things that already exist. Assets and the register An asset is a physical component that delivers a service: a bridge, a pumping station, a pipe, a sign. Managing them starts with an asset register, a structured inventory giving every item an identifier, location, attributes, condition, criticality, value and history. - Hierarchy matters — network, facility, component — because decisions are made at different levels. - A register is only useful if current, so ownership and update rules matter more than the software. Condition assessment Condition is judged by inspection: routine visual checks, detailed inspections, and special investigations after damage. Inspectors record distress against a defined scale, such as 1 to 5, with photographs and measurements; a rating only means something if everyone applies the same definitions. - Non-destructive tests — cover meters, half-cell potential, ultrasonic thickness — add evidence without opening the structure. - Sampling is inevitable, so results are estimates with a confidence range, not facts. Deterioration Assets decline in different ways. Corrosion, fatigue, abrasion, settlement and weathering all depend on age, loading, environment and maintenance history, so two identical components can age very differently. - Deterioration models are probabilistic: a Markov model gives the probability of moving from one condition state to another in a period. - Survival curves describe the fraction still serviceable at each age. - Models support timing decisions, but they are only as good as the inspection data behind them. Markov condition transition C(t+1) = Ct · P Reliability, availability and failure rates Reliability asks how long an asset works before it fails. For a fleet, mean time between failures is total running time divided by the number of failures, and its inverse is the failure rate. Availability combines reliability with repairability through mean time to repair: an asset that fails rarely but takes months to fix can be less available than one that fails often and is repaired in hours. - Components in series multiply their availabilities: ten links at 99% each is at best about 90% available — parallel redundancy buys the extra nines. - Quote MTBF with its maintenance context, because a design change or deferred servicing moves it more than the equipment itself does. Mean time between failures MTBF = operating time / failures Failure rate λ = 1 / MTBF Availability A = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR) Series availability A = A1 · A2 · … · An Maintenance strategies Maintenance ranges from reactive (fix it when it breaks) through planned preventive (service on a calendar) and condition-based (act when inspection shows a threshold) to predictive (act when data suggests failure is approaching). The options for an asset are usually do nothing, repair, rehabilitate or replace. - Reactive work is cheap until a failure closes a road or a water main. - Preventive work is predictable but may replace healthy parts. - Condition-based work needs reliable monitoring. Strategy Trigger Strength Weakness Level of service and performance measurement Assets are funded to deliver a level of service, so management needs measures that describe the service, not the asset. For a road: travel time, roughness and closures; for water: pressure, interruptions and response time. A performance indicator turns raw data into a comparable number, and a target turns it into a decision. - Customer minutes lost multiplies incidents by duration and customers affected. - Backlog is the share of the network below its condition target. - Report indicators with their trend, not just this year's number — a network can look fine this quarter while the backlog quietly compounds. subjects.summary: How models learn patterns from data, and how to tell whether one is any good. It covers regression, classification, validation, the metrics that match a real question, overfitting, neural networks and the ethics of deploying a model.
subjects.text: How models learn patterns from data, and how to tell whether one is any good. It covers regression, classification, validation, the metrics that match a real question, overfitting, neural networks and the ethics of deploying a model. Learning is fitting a function Machine learning fits a function from examples instead of writing rules by hand. - Supervised learning: each example carries a label; regression predicts a number, classification a category. - Unsupervised methods look for structure without labels — clustering, dimension reduction. - Reinforcement learning learns actions from reward. The estimate is only as good as the sample: biased or unrepresentative data produce a confident model that is wrong in deployment. Regression and classification Linear regression fits a straight line to a numeric outcome by least squares; the error term collects what the line misses. For a yes/no decision, logistic regression passes a linear score through the sigmoid to give a probability between 0 and 1. The score defines a boundary at zero; the output is a probability, not a verdict. A threshold converts it into a class, trading false positives against false negatives. Linear regression y = β₀ + β₁ x + ε Logistic (sigmoid) model p = 1 / (1 + e^(−s)), s = w·x + b Training: loss and gradients Training chooses parameters that make predictions close to the labels. - A loss function measures the gap — squared error for regression, cross-entropy for classification. - Gradient descent nudges each weight against the gradient of the loss. - The learning rate is the critical choice: too small and training crawls, too large and the loss jumps around or diverges. - Mini-batches trade noisy gradients for speed; one pass over the data is an epoch. Gradient descent update w ← w − η ∂L/∂w Validation and leakage A model scored on the data it learned from is marking its own homework. Split into training, validation and test sets; fit on training, choose hyperparameters on validation, and touch the test set once at the end. k-fold cross-validation rotates the validation fold so the estimate uses every row. Leakage is the silent killer: scaling before the split, duplicate records across sets, or features recorded after the outcome. Time-ordered data must be split by time, not at random. Stratified split and fit Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = traintestsplit(X, y, testsize=0.2, stratify=y) model.fit(Xtr, ytr) score = model.score(Xte, yte) Metrics that match the question Accuracy is the first metric and often the wrong one. With 1,000 cases of which 60 are positive, a model that always says no scores 94% accuracy and catches nothing. - A confusion matrix separates true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives, from which precision and recall follow. - F1 balances the two, while ROC-AUC measures ranking across all thresholds. - Regression metrics differ: RMSE penalises large errors, MAE keeps the original units, and R² is the variation explained. Precision and recall precision = TP / (TP + FP), recall = TP / (TP + FN) F1 score F1 = 2 · precision · recall / (precision + recall) Metric What it answers Trap if used alone Overfitting and regularisation Overfitting is learning the training set rather than the pattern: training error keeps falling while validation error rises. It comes from a model that is too flexible for the amount of data. The cure is more data, a simpler model, or regularisation that adds a penalty for large weights. Dropout, early stopping and augmentation are other forms of restraint. Underfitting is the opposite failure, and no amount of tuning fixes a model that cannot express the pattern. Regularised loss (L2) Lreg = L + λ Σ w² Neural networks A neural network stacks layers of weighted sums and non-linear activations; depth lets it represent interactions that a linear model cannot. ReLU is the common activation, and backpropagation computes the gradients that gradient descent needs. Convolutional layers exploit local structure
